Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals a comprehensive picture of their spatial distribution. By analyzing nearly 19,000 detected particles with energies exceeding 4 EeV, primarily through air shower observations, we identified localized anisotropies likely resulting from extragalactic sources such as supermassive black hole mergers within gigaparsec-distance galaxies. We discovered concentrated patterns of cosmic rays in the northern celestial hemisphere, corresponding to specific sky areas with enhanced particle densities sometimes exceeding 10-sigma significance levels. These areas tend to converge with renowned cosmic ray hotspots observed by other detectors but with greater spatial resolution, and primarily point towards active galactic nuclei hosting accreting black holes. Additionally, we found evidence of oriented anisotropies along the Milky Way galaxy disk, which could be explained by a source direction dependence influenced by the detector's side acceptance. We also identified a focal point in the southern celestial hemisphere unlikely to be caused by cosmic ray anisotropies alone, which may be related to a local source or atmospheric system effect influencing the detector's response. By focusing on the most anisotropic patterns and excluding localized areas pointing towards specific galaxies, we estimated the total number of high-energy cosmic rays originating from such localized sources within the observable universe to be approximately 200-500. These findings highlight the complex and anisotropic nature of high-energy cosmic ray sources, suggesting that a diverse set of extragalactic objects with different mass accretion rates can contribute to the high-energy cosmic ray flux. Lastly, we discussed detection pathways for some specific sources and discussed the potential for future detectors to deeply penetrate the Milky Way galaxy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by developing a dataset, called CLEVR-MT, which comprises multi-modal descriptions and 3D objects with varying orientations. Recently, 6DoF object pose estimation has been advanced by combining 2D detection and 3D pose regression through correspondence learning between predicted 3D coordinates and actual object points. This method requires a substantial number of 3D annotations, a significant barrier for large-scale real-world applications. To address this challenge, the proposal focuses on a special case where only 2D annotations are provided, assuming a fixed orientation for objects. A novel framework, named DeepHMap++, is presented to accurately determine 6DoF poses without pre-existing 3D annotations. It leverages a unique clustering method based on projection characteristics to generate compact 3D models from scratch, which serve as proxy targets for correspondence learning. The proposed DeepHMap++ model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the BOP Challenge, a renowned benchmark in the field. Moreover, extensive experiments on the LS3D dataset demonstrate its superiority over competing methods. The code for DeepHMap++ is publicly available at https://github.com/lingyu-92/DeepHMap++.

Our research expands the eigenvector method to identify prominent nodes within multi-layered networks by taking into account the mutual influence of significant nodes across different layers. In each network layer, a separate eigenvector calculation is performed to determine the significance of nodes relative to their connections within that specific layer. These eigenvector calculations are then combined across layers, using a variation of the Clauset method that accounts for the degree of cross-talk between layers. This combined eigenvector approach enables us to identify nodes that stand out across multiple layers and can be particularly useful in identifying central components that span different layers of a multi-scale system. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital characteristics. For the iron atoms in both trimer and terminally-coordinated sites, we find substantial gaps in the density of states. However, for the intermediate-coordinated site, we find these gaps do not exist, which could be related to the experimentally observed spectral features and intermediate-valence behavior. Additionally, we find that the trimer sites exhibit localized, half-filled t2g orbitals and magnetization primarily within these sites. This, along with the absence of direct iron-iron bonding, could be responsible for the lack of magnetic coupling between the trimer sites. We also explore the effects of external pressures and lattice distortions on the electronic structure and localization of the intermediate-coordinated site. Along with the naturally occurring variants, we examine defect models of the trimer sites which exhibit different behavior, both with and without direct iron-iron bonding, as well as with and without the intermediate-coordinated site, which displays either displaced or absent peaks in the density of states. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the electromagnetic tensor and the Weyl curvature tensor. This article provides a concise review of how bivectors are employed to represent these important physical concepts within the framework of Newman-Penrose formalism. We examine the explicit expressions of the Weyl curvature tensor and the electromagnetic tensor in terms of bivectors, demonstrating their direct relationship. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the Papapetrou field equations and the Einstein field equations using the Newman-Penrose formalism. Additionally, this review includes an analysis of the complex conformal field theory and the Einstein field equations in the Newman-Penrose formalism. We also provide appendices detailing the background material, including the principles of the Newman-Penrose formalism, the complex conjugate of multivectors, and the complex conjugate of the Weyl tensor. This review is intended for researchers interested in the Newman-Penrose formalism and complex conformal geometry. This work was previously published in the journal "Pramana - Journal of Physics".

Early detection is crucial for esophageal cancer, a highly lethal disease with a poor five-year survival rate.  CT scans are a readily available tool for this early detection, with radiologists relying on visual inspection to identify neoplasms.  However, research has shown that even experienced radiologists can be misled by certain neoplasm characteristics such as variation in density and the presence of lymph nodes.  To enhance this process, a neural network called the Dense Focus Unet was developed to automatically segment neoplasms from CT scans of the esophagus.  This model includes focal and global components to analyze both high-frequency features and low-frequency background information.  By scaling the model for three different density ranges, it can effectively handle the variability of neoplasms.  To evaluate the model, it was applied to data from two different hospitals, with results showing a moderate to substantial level of agreement with expert radiologists.  Further analysis of the model's performance based on patient data was challenging due to limitations in data availability.  Nevertheless, this model demonstrates potential as a radiomic tool to aid in the early detection of esophageal cancer.  Future work should focus on refining the model and scaling it up to handle more varied and extensive datasets.  This includes exploring different network architectures and sampling methods to improve performance and reduce memory requirements. Code-mixed languages, which combine scripts from different languages, are a common mode of online communication for multilingual communities, offering a wealth of information for social media monitoring, user engagement analysis, and sentiment mining, among other tasks. Yet, developing effective NLP methods to handle code-mixed data has been hindered by several challenges. Firstly, the absence of a well-defined grammar and vocabulary for code-mixed languages makes it difficult to create accurate tokenizers and part-of-speech taggers. Secondly, many NLP tasks rely heavily on pretrained models, which have limited performance when applied to code-mixed data due to their reliance on monolingual pretraining. Thirdly, evaluation metrics for these tasks are often based on the characteristics of the target languages, neglecting the distinct features of code-mixed data. In response to these limitations, this work seeks to explore factors that influence the effectiveness of NLP methods for multilingual communities, with a focus on code-mixed languages. We investigate several factors, including the source languages of the code-mixed data, the degree of mixing present, and the linguistic characteristics of the codes used, among others. By examining these factors, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of the obstacles and challenges facing NLP for multilingual communities and identify potential solutions to address these challenges. In particular, we find that models trained on multilingual datasets perform better when the code-mixed data is primarily based on the same source language, while models trained on monolingual datasets exhibit similar performance regardless of the source languages used. We also find that models performed better on mixed texts with a higher frequency of certain words and names. Our research suggests integrating named entity recognition into NLP tasks can lead to better performance. Finally, we find that models performed better on mixed texts with simpler grammar structures. Despite this difficulty, robots can significantly benefit from learning to process such descriptions, enabling them to learn from visual demonstrations combined with audio feedback. In this work, we investigate how robots can process and understand audio descriptions of humans performing tasks in front of them. To achieve this, we gathered a large dataset of a person providing instructions to a robot while performing various manipulation activities. Furthermore, we explore the integration of this model into a learning framework from visual demonstrations, enabling it to correct any discrepancies between the described and observed scenes. The resulting system is put to the test on a set of challenging scenarios, promising substantial performance gains over a baseline model. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often employed to address problems with multiple sparsity domains. However, most existing methods overlook the comprehensive analysis of varied sparsity domains and tend to focus mainly on overlapping areas between two domains. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that addresses a problem involving multiple sparsity domains. The aim of this framework is to concurrently handle multiple sparsity domains with varying levels of data density and item overlap. To effectively handle diverse sparsity domains, MSDCR extracts specific aspects of user preferences from multiple sparsity domains and combines them through a thorough preference learning method. Furthermore, MSDCR incorporates a memory network and a rating prediction model to obtain the aspect weights and predict ratings, respectively. The performance of MSDCR is demonstrated through extensive experiments using real-world datasets, and the findings are compared with existing state-of-the-art CDR methods. Moreover, MSDCR is shown to outperform existing methods in multiple sparsity domains. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/lingyu-gh/MSDCR. The results obtained from real-world datasets validate the superiority of MSDCR. The proposed solution can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as recommending movies across multiple sparsity domains and electing leaders in organizations with varying sparsity among voting members. The proposed solution provides an outstanding cross-domain recommendation performance even when there are few items in common between domains. The challenge of movie recommendation across multiple sparsity domains is used as an exemplary application in the paper. The paper presents a detailed analysis of a real-world dataset for movie recommendations across multiple sparsity domains and presents a memory network-based solution to guide this research further. The proposed solution can be extended to recommend leaders in organizations with varying sparsity among voting members by incorporating additional features related to the candidate's position and electability. The paper presents a novel framework called MSDFR for recommending leaders in organizations with varying sparsity among voting members and presents experimental results obtained using real-world datasets. The proposed solution can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as providing personalized product recommendations across multiple sparsity domains and electing leaders in organizations with varying sparsity among voting members. The proposed solution provides an outstanding cross-domain recommendation performance even when there are few items in common between domains. The challenge of providing personalized product recommendations across multiple sparity domains is used as an exemplary application

Conic programming is a versatile method that can be used to solve a wide range of optimization problems, including linear, second-order, semi-definite, and nonlinear issues. Due to its versatility, conic formulations have become very popular across various fields. Nonetheless, one area where conic formulations have seen little adoption is in the study of organic compounds, specifically organic conic formulations. To address this, a new version of the Hypatia.jl library is introduced, capable of automatically generating conic formulations for organic compounds based on the principles of conic physics. This version of Hypatia.jl leverages the CONIC.jl solver to the same extent as the initial release, enabling users to generate conic formulations and validate them using the Z3 solver. Moreover, it provides a straightforward and general approach to create conic formulations for organic compounds, thereby expanding the scope of problems that can be tackled with the Hypatia.jl framework. As an illustration of this method's value, a nonlinear Hamiltonian operator is formulated and the resulting operator confirmed to be accurate through comparisons with established methods. This new version of Hypatia.jl is available under the MIT open-source license. The library, solvers, and examples are readily downloadable from https://github.com/organicchemistry/Hypatia.jl/releases/tag/v0.2.0. A concise user guide is also provided in the repository. The Hypatia.jl framework is designed to address a broad range of optimization problems in the field of organic chemistry. The development of this framework is ongoing, with future enhancements aimed at expanding the range of problems it can tackle. The steady advancement of MRI technology necessitates regular quality control to ensure patient safety and effective data collection. As new MRI systems and sequences emerge, it's essential to establish protocols for assessing their reliability. Currently, there is no widely accepted standard for evaluating the quality of MRI data, and quality assurance processes vary significantly between institutions. To address this challenge, researchers propose using deep learning techniques to train models that can accurately identify low-quality MRI data, with the goal of providing a standardized framework for quality assessment. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the authors used public MRI datasets to train and test a model capable of distinguishing between poor-quality and acceptable data. This model can be used to evaluate the reliability of MRI data across various applications, including 3D brain reconstruction shown here. Given the limited scope of available MRI data, particularly in relation to new MRI systems and sequences, generalizing the model to perform dimensionally, such as to assess the quality of PET-MRI acquisitions, remains a significant challenge. To achieve this, the authors employed a transfer learning approach using publicly available MRI datasets to train models for evaluating the quality of PET-MRI data on various systems, including a case study with a dimension that includes multiple MRI sequences. This research showcases the potential of deep learning for MRI quality assurance and provides a foundation for further generalization efforts. To advance this work, the authors are contributing their MRI quality assessment model and datasets in response to the need for standardized quality assurance protocols. This initiative aims to accelerate the development of generalizable models for evaluating the quality of MRI data across various dimensions through collaborative research. This collaboration is facilitated through the open-source MRI quality assurance repository on GitHub. To contribute to this project, please visit <https://github.com/quality-mri>. The number of automated agents operating in a mutual interest is steadily increasing, and their interconnection is becoming more complex. As a result, there's a growing need to create scalable frameworks that can efficiently manage large-scale, dynamic automated meetings. Current methods often prioritize speedy decision-making over optimal outcomes but offer limited practical application. In contrast, we present a novel approach, MARMID, capable of facilitating collaborative automation across various domains by leveraging reinforcement learning within the context of meeting protocols. This general-purpose system enables diverse agents to collaborate and exchange information during meetings, with the potential to integrate additional protocols easily. Empirical testing demonstrates MARMID's versatility and the effectiveness of its incentive mechanism in promoting cooperative behavior among agents. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential practical use of MARMID in complex, real-world scenarios, such as peer-to-peer energy trading. The code for MARMID is available at https://github.com/AAAI-2023-marmid.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of the novel tin-based GdSn3, CmSn3 compounds and a proposed alloy Cm0.5Gd0.5Sn3 using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. Calculations were performed to analyze how the magnetic moment, electronic density of states, and crystal structure of these compounds respond to U and e.g. lattice parameters. Our results show that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds possess a tetragonal crystal structure with an anti-ferromagnetic arrangement of magnetic moments. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the band gap of the CmSn3 compound is direct/indirect and that the alloy Cm0.5Gd0.5Sn3 exhibits anti-ferromagnetic behavior similar to its parent compounds. Lastly, our study discovered that the electronic density of states of both compounds is composed of local and semi-localized states. Lastly, we conclude that these compounds and the proposed alloy could have applications in spintronic devices due to their unique half-metallic and semi-conductive properties.

We've developed a method for using weak lensing convergence to enhance Type Ia Supernovae data, specifically applying it to the Pantheon SN Ia sample. Convergence causes a characteristic distortion in the shape of galaxies, making their apparent size more substantial than their actual size. As a result, more distant objects are magnified more significantly. We calculated this effect for each galaxy associated with a supernova in the Pantheon dataset, based on its photometric properties and positional relationship to the supernova. We then incorporated this information by calculating the convergence at the location of each supernova using weak lensing techniques and the publicly available KiDS weak lensing map as a proxy. We found this approach to be feasible and promising, with several potential advantages including but not limited to, the ability to incorporate additional information from the host galaxies. Furthermore, as the relationship between the lensing effect and the galaxy properties is calculable but also complex, we employed machine learning to model this relationship. Leveraging the KiDS lensing map's high resolution, with a smoothing length set to 4.5 arcminutes, we incorporated the information into the SN Ia distance modulus, resulting in a 0.16 mag reduction in the overall scatter. Notably, this approach is independent of the standard cosmological parameters, relying instead on the intrinsic properties of the galaxies and the local structure of the universe. As such, it complements the standard cosmological analysis using the dark matter halos surrounding the supernovae hosts. We also explored the contribution of the lensing effect from the mass distribution within the hosts themselves, based on the Tully-Fisher relation, as well as the influence of the lensing effect on the supernova photometry, finding no such impact. Finally, we highlighted the promise of this method for future surveys with more comprehensive KiDS-style lensing maps and deeper galaxy surveys with more precise galaxy property measurements. As such, it has the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of future SN Ia cosmology investigations. The development of efficient and compact light management systems is a pressing need to overcome the challenges of large-scale integrated photonic networks. To this end, we propose a novel T-shaped resonator, which allows for the creation of a 4-fold reduction in the number of necessary etalon layers when implementing a 4-channel multiplexing demonstration. Furthermore, this T-shaped resonator can be seamlessly integrated into a 2D photonic chip utilizing the foundry's standard process, and has been tested to function properly across a wide spectral range, from 1500 to 1600 nanometers. With its compact design, this T-shaped resonator has significant potential applications in complex light management systems, and my findings are relevant to a broad range of semiconductor materials, including silicon.

For our work, we are using a unique context that is present outside the main object of interest and assess how effectively state-of-the-art object detection methods are able to locate this external context. Deep learning models have achieved high performance in various object detection tasks but often struggle with contextual understanding. To demonstrate this challenge, we are using a specially designed dataset that contains both a primary and secondary object within the same image. By evaluating the external context of this dataset, we found that current object detection models are primarily focused on identifying the main object and do not adequately capture the surrounding context. To further improve context-aware object detection, we propose a simple yet effective evaluation framework that incorporates external context along with the primary object of interest. By utilizing this context, we are also exploring the relationship between objects within the same image. To validate our approach, we are using a publicly available dataset with both primary and secondary objects but did not find a significant difference in the performance of current object detection models when comparing the presence of the secondary object to the absence of that object. Nonetheless, our context assessment framework has the potential to reveal underlying challenges in object detection tasks and can also explore the relationship between objects within the same image. To facilitate this discovery, we are providing pre-trained models along with our context assessment framework for other researchers to use. We examine the concentrations of binary random variables with a negative correlation property. Let's consider two independently generated random vectors, one from an exponential distribution with n dimensions and another from a Dirichlet distribution with n+1 dimensions, both with parameter 1. These vectors represent binary random variables when their corresponding values are mapped to the set {-1, 1}. We establish that the sum of these binary random variables follows a binomial distribution with n parameters, and using this information, we derive concentration bounds for the sum of binary random variables with a negative correlation property. Ultimately, these results imply that the sum of these binary random variables exhibits strong concentration, i.e., the sum's absolute value remains bounded by a polynomial of order O(n1/2) with a small constant, and this estimate is precise to within a logarithmic factor. Additionally, these findings enable us to generalize the results to include weighted sums of these binary random variables, thereby extending the concentration disparities to weighted sums. Finally, these general results also encompass the specialized case of the concentration disparities for the number of successes in Bernoulli trials with a negative correlation property. The negative correlation property in question can be either given or inferred from the distribution of the binary random variables. The paper's last section highlights its main contributions. This research introduces a hybrid level set / embedded boundary method to resolve problems related to melting and freezing. This technique combines the level set method's ability to model moving boundaries with the embedded boundary method's capability to easily integrate boundary conditions within the computational domain. By integrating the level set and embedded boundary methods, we developed a numerical approach using a conservative and conservative-form semi-implicit scheme to resolve the conservation equations. This technique was effectively tested and applied to model problems related to melting and freezing, including a Rayleigh-Benard instability test, Darcy's law with a moving interface, and a Stefan problem with accumulation and evaporation. Furthermore, we integrated the level set method with the embedded boundary technique into the COMPLEXFluid toolbox made available with this article. This research was published in the journal Computers and Structures, volume 88. Lastly, we discuss the hybrid level set / embedded boundary method and its potential applications, including chemical reactions, phase changes, and material removal processes. In multiagent competitions, having multiple equilibria can make it challenging to evaluate learning agents, especially when there's a desire to distinguish between "rational" and "irrational" behavior. We introduce a new metric, centered on a concept called the "rationalizable equilibrium," to address this issue. This statistical measure assesses the performance of agents at each equilibrium mode equally and calculates the share of time spent at high-payoff states when playing optimally against other agents at the corresponding rationalizable equilibrium. To apply this metric in a general setting, we develop two learning algorithms: one for identifying the mode corresponding to the highest payoff at each equilibrium, and another that combines this with a rational learning strategy to visit states that offer the highest payoff when playing optimally against other agents at the rationalizable equilibrium. We evaluate these methods in multiagent competitions with multiple equilibria and find they outperform various baseline methods. When comparing our proposed methods to baselines, we use a new performance metric that calculates the expected payoff at the rationalizable equilibrium as the primary evaluation criterion, in addition to conventional metrics. Our results are consistent across multiple datasets, including generated datasets and those derived from real-world data related to the game of Tetris. We also explore how our proposed methods perform when there are fewer equilibria by introducing a variant of the Tetris game with fewer possible actions. Our research demonstrates that it's possible to acquire a rationalizable equilibrium in a single-agent setup with multiple equilibria by employing a simple learning algorithm, and we provide explicit conditions under which this occurs. We further investigate the relationship between our results and existing research on logistic regression and provide a mathematical expression characterizing this relationship. Finally, we develop a general procedure for validating the performance of agents at each equilibrium mode equally and discuss how this validates the rationalizable equilibrium metric. We conclude by exploring the potential applications of our research, including evaluating learning agents in multiagent competitions with multiple equilibria. Lastly, we provide code related to our research. A key factor in preventing the spread of an epidemic on a contact network is the identification of robust core components that cannot be compromised without significantly impacting the network's overall structure. In this study, we develop and analyze an evolutionary model where two individuals whose infection becomes apparent rewire the network to prevent similar super-spreader infections. We demonstrate that networks evolved through this process converge to a state characterized by isolated components that resemble "cliques." A Monte Carlo Markov Chain algorithm is used to simulate this model, and our analytical findings are validated through these numerical experiments. We also introduce a simplified random graph model with similar properties, which provides an insight into the fundamental mechanisms governing the model's behavior. The analysis of this model reveals specific parameters that influence the emergence of complete subgraphs and our simulations confirm these predictions. The model is further applied to investigate how networks evolve in response to changing epidemic risks and the effects of "friendly" connections on the network. The simulation results also demonstrate that networks evolved through this model are resistant to certain flaws, such as the presence of orphan nodes. The model's potential uses are discussed, along with its connections to existing research in statistics and mathematics. The associated code is available online. I demonstrate how our theoretical framework can be combined with experimental data, and show that it accurately describes the relationship between neutrino and antineutrino scattering, even for processes that involve multiple significant sub-processes.  Furthermore, we find that our method outperforms the traditional method of combining data for the same lepton type.  To apply this framework to antineutrino scattering, we must first analyze neutrino scattering data for the same process.  This involves studying the dependencies of cross-sections on energy, scattering angle, and quark mass.  Since our framework is independent of specific proton structure models, we fit our theoretical predictions to data from four different processes at six energy facilities, using both combined and individual data sets.  These fits enable us to accurately predict the relationships between neutrino and antineutrino scattering, as well as the behavior of cross-sections at different energy and scattering angle scales.  They also provide the necessary inputs for adjusting proton structure functions, and demonstrate how our method can be applied to antineutrino scattering processes at facilities that have only neutrino scattering data.  To validate our results, we compared our fitted predictions with the characteristics of neutral current scattering processes at two facilities, and found them to be accurate. To improve policy enhancement methods, particularly reinforcement learning enhancements using experience replay, we propose a new exploration strategy that is designed to increase the variance of returns observed during exploration.  This new strategy is called Variance-Aware Experience Replay (VAER).  We hypothesize that VAER will result in more accurate policy assessments and greater overall performance compared to existing methods.  To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a series of experiments using both discrete and continuous control domains and found that VAER generally outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods.  Our findings also reveal that VAER is particularly effective when the size of the replay buffer is small.  We further investigate the relationship between VAER and existing methods by modifying the challenge design to make it comparable with a prior art.  Additionally, we discuss two approaches to further improve VAER and demonstrate their value in specific scenarios.  Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulghul93/VAER.  We believe that VAER can be used as a building block to develop a wide range of exploration strategies that prioritize the discovery of challenging experiences. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we encounter side-branches that don't lead to explicit user objectives. Current state-of-the-art approaches typically focus on direct paths to the desired outcome, neglecting the significance of these side-branches in real-life conversations. We argue that ignoring these branches results in flawed evaluations and inadequate models, as they fail to demonstrate crucial aspects of dialogue intelligence, such as detecting deception or discussing sensitive topics. To rectify this shortcoming, we introduce a new dataset, Conversational Crossover, which features dialogue sub-branches indicating a change in topic or a shift in user intent. We also propose a corresponding challenge, Crossover Detection, where models must identify these sub-branches. To solve this challenge, we developed a highly-branching dialogue framework, MultiTalk, and demonstrated its effectiveness through a series of experiments. Our findings show that MultiTalk outperforms existing approaches on Conversational Crossover tasks, even when evaluating models using existing datasets without side-branches. Consequently, we advocate for more diverse and complex evaluation datasets that incorporate varied branching structures in dialogue systems. With this in mind, we are releasing Conversational Crossover along with MultiTalk, hoping it will contribute to more rigorous assessments of dialogue models. Moreover, we provide detailed guidance on implementing and evaluating this framework, along with multiple available code repositories to facilitate further development. Moreover, we present a simplified version of the dataset, removal of branches without a clear change in topic or user intent, as an easily manageable benchmark for evaluation models. Lastly, we are open to collaborations that can further explore MultiTalk and Conversational Crossover in dialogue systems.

This mapping is achieved by translating the statistical properties of random log-gases on the real line into the geometric behavior of multiple SLEs, leveraging the Corti-Kenneth extension of the Riemann-Hilbert problem to non-integer parameters. As a result, we obtain a collection of independent imaginary parts whose sum equals 2, which can be viewed as a discrete version of the multiple SLE case. This discrete model allows us to explore multiple SLE with internal marks at non-integer parameters. Furthermore, we investigate multiple SLE with geometrically changing parameters and prove that its ending point behaves like a discrete model with independent imaginary parts whose sum equals 2. This research aims to advance the understanding of how turbulent jet fires interact with vulnerable structures, particularly those made of metal, by modeling the reaction of a jet fire to acoustic excitation in a linearized structure. To this end, a unique experimental setup was devised where a flame is sustained above an open window, with acoustic waves generated above the window to mimic the vibrations of a metal structure. To better understand the relationship between the flame and the acoustic waves, a novel "active flame method" was developed for marking the hottest parts of the flame, thus allowing the identification of heat transfer pathways from the window to the surrounding environment. As a result, it became clear that acoustic waves can disrupt the recirculation zone within the flame, leading to the formation of turbulent eddies that foster heat transfer through convection and radiation. To further investigate this phenomenon, a numerical analysis was performed using ANSYS Fluent, with the recirculation zone found to be particularly prone to destruction by turbulent eddies in the inner cavity of the jet fire. A subclass of such interactions allows neutrino oscillations to be affected in a way that varies with position, leading to oscillations in neutrino spectra within solar systems and planetary bodies composed of dark matter. These interactions also impact neutrinoless double beta decay, either lengthening or shortening its half-life depending on the type of interaction, and we establish a lower bound on half-lives based on current measurements. We introduce a theoretical framework for nonlocal gravity, referred to as Nonlocal Gravitation Theory (NGT), with the aim of incorporating gravitation as a complex conjoined process involving both the spacetime environment and material objects themselves. In this framework, gravitation is viewed as a relational phenomenon born from interactions between objects and their surrounding spacetime. Since NGT considers spacetime as a relational aspect of the gravitational interaction, it does not treat spacetime as a background entity. Instead, NGT formulates spacetime as a dynamical, relational, and emergent trait of the interaction between objects and their constituent parts. Since NGT does not treat spacetime as a background, there is no geometric interpretation of the theory in traditional terms. However, we can re-express the NGT formalism in a way that resembles General Relativity, with the addition of new terms representing nonlocal effects. In this modified form, the NGT parameters are incorporated into modified connection and metric tensors, which we refer to as constitutive connections and metrological tensors. These tensors are distinct from their conventional counterparts in modified General Relativity scenarios. In the modified NGT formulation, we find that the nonlocal effects behave as conservative contributions to mass-energy. In the context of scalar gravity, with minimal nonlocal interactions, we derive an analytical solution for the massless field part, which allows us to identify the nonlocal effects as contributing to the generation of massive particles. In the modified NGT formulation, we also recover the massless, nonlocal field component through the introduction of a nontrivial conformal rescaling of the metrological tensor. This conformal rescaling is a purely relational trait born from the interaction between objects and their constituent parts. In the process, we demonstrate that the nonlocal effects behave as conservative contributions to mass-energy, which is also recoverable through a nontrivial conformal rescaling of the metrological tensor. This behavior is found to hold in both scalar and tensorial representations of the nonlocal gravity field. In the tensorial representation, with linear nonlocal interactions, we derive an analytical solution for the massless field part, which allows us to identify the nonlocal effects as contributing to the generation of massive, spin-2 particles. The majority of bulge LMXBs exhibit rare, long-interval X-ray bursts, suggesting long duty cycles or binary systems with low mass retention.  The population of bulge LMXBs also displays a lack of repeated bursts from the same source within a certain time frame, referred to as the "repetition gap".  By defining this gap as exceeding 10 years, only a small subset of the bulge LMXBs meet this criterion, primarily consisting of low-luminosity X-ray binaries associated with the Galactic Centre.  The remaining sources within the bulge, including the most active low-mass X-ray binaries, fail to do so.  The repetition gap serves as a distinguishing feature for identifying dormant LMXBs in the Milky Way bulge, with the majority being situated in the disk rather than the bulge.  This finding is supported by the presence of a large number of bulge LMXBs in the disk, with many positioned near the solar neighborhood.  The repetition gap also offers insights into the lifetime of low-mass X-ray binaries, with the majority surviving for over 10 million years before undergoing supernovae explosions. Understanding the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences relies on varying levels of semantic detail.  This study demonstrates how natural language inference can distinguish between different levels of semantic analysis.  A neural network trained on natural language inference tasks distinguishes between, for example, the related sentences "The company is profitable" and "The company is financially successful."  However, this distinction does not arise from the network's knowledge of linguistic rules but rather from the inherent properties of the inference data.  By manipulating the inference data, we show that a pre-trained language model like BERT can distinguish between, for example, the sentences "Papers are submitted" and "Papers submit themselves."  We also explore BERT's performance on infinitely complex semantic relationships.  This research provides a straightforward method for evaluating the complexity of a dataset's semantic variety and shows that this variety is not unique to one dataset but is a general property of natural language inference.  We further investigate the relationship between this semantic variety and linguistic phenomena like anaphora by demonstrating how BERT's performance declines when comparing, for example, "The company established itself" and "The company established John."  We conclude by discussing the implications of this research for the ongoing debate over lexical semantics and compositional semantics.  We complement this discussion with a simple mathematical model that captures the essential features of semantic variety in discourse.  This model enables controlled experimentation with the properties of inference data and provides a framework for integrating natural language inference with other cognitive tasks that involve discourse.  This research is accompanied by a freely available dataset that includes the semantic analyses used to derive the variety in question.  This dataset can be used as a starting point for the ongoing project of developing a quantitative measure of the complexity of semantic relationships.  This research also introduces a related challenge: designing a suitable evaluation metric for the complexity of semantic relationships.  This challenge is reflected in the accompanying challenge at the CLEF 2023 conference. The current study focuses on a particular aspect of vertex division, namely bipartite division, where a graph is divided into two separate components: one containing independent vertices and another composed of connected components that form a perfect matching within each part. A key problem associated with bipartite division is identifying whether a given graph can be divided in this manner. We establish that a field of fractions arises from a non-void set of rational functions, provided that residue mapping can be applied to all polynomials. This condition can be met when the coefficients of polynomials come from a field that contains no positive divisors other than itself. As a result, we are able to generalize the concept of integral domains with unique factorization properties to their associated fields of fractions. Specifically, a field of fractions $\Omega$ is considered 'integral' if it contains a subset of rational functions $\Gamma$ such that $\Omega$ is generated by $\Gamma$ and for any two distinct rational functions $f/g$ and $h/k$ in $\Gamma$, their least common multiple divided by their greatest common divisor is equivalent to $f_{1}h_{1}/(g_{1}k_{1})$ for some irreducible factors $f_{1}, g_{1}$ of $f$ and $g$, as well as $h_{1}, k_{1}$ of $h$ and $k$. Notably, this leads to the conclusion that fields with unique factorization properties are also known as 'Pellian' fields. Furthermore, we establish criteria for fields that are 'integral' and provide examples of fields that are 'integral' or 'Pellian'. Additionally, we examine the relationship between 'integral' fields and fields that are 'Pellian' and show that they share many characteristics, although they are not equivalent. It is also demonstrated that fields with unique factorization properties are infinite fields. Moreover, we provide a more general definition of 'integral' fields that can be applied to fields that are based on Euclidean domains rather than polynomial rings. As a result, we are able to demonstrate that certain fields that are derived from Euclidean domains do not have unique factorization properties. Finally, we examine the relationship between 'integral' fields and fields that are based on Euclidean domains and provide examples of fields that are derived from Euclidean domains. It is also demonstrated that there are fields that are not 'Pellian' or 'integral', in addition to fields that are derived from Euclidean domains. Moreover, we establish that there are fields that are not 'Pellian' or 'integral' if and only if there are fields that are not derived from Euclidean domains. Our research examines a specific type of graph, which we call an "avalanche graph," and explores its structure using percolation theory. Aavalanche graphs arise from the application of a linear transformation to vectors within a well-defined boundary, and these graphs have been utilized in various contexts, including cryptography, physics, and mathematics. A crucial matrix, the Gram matrix, is determined, and its properties are such that it allows for the efficient generation of avalanche graphs through random linear transformations. Furthermore, we derive the distribution of the Gram matrix's eigenvalues, which in turn dictates the characteristics of the associated Markov chain. This chain can be either ergodic or multi-ergodic, depending on specific conditions being met. Ergodicity is associated with a uniform distribution of states, whereas multi-ergodicity yields a distribution that is governed by a mixture of uniform distributions. This finding is particularly notable from a theoretical perspective because it demonstrates that there is no fundamental limitation precluding the use of small-scale quantum systems in various applications. This achievement also surpasses the previously reported results by offering a more comprehensive understanding of the distribution of eigenvalues and the associated Markov chain's behavior. Lastly, we discussed the potential applications of our research in small MIMO systems, with line-of-sight conditions, and highlighted the paper's contributions in three key areas.

A key challenge in the integration of renewable energy sources lies in managing the discretionary components of our energy system, such as storage and demand response. To efficiently achieve this, self-scheduling algorithms can be utilized by individual entities. However, these algorithms often rely on perfect knowledge of future markets, which can be difficult to obtain, especially in decentralized systems lacking a central authority. This paper presents a robust self-scheduling approach for energy storage in decentralized markets. Unlike existing methods, it accommodates uncertainty in prices and supply/demand, using robust optimization to ensure that discrete markets remain non-negative and to provide valid price intervals for renewal probabilities. A key advantage of this approach is that it precludes the necessity of learning models that predict prices and renewal probabilities. Instead, it generates storage settings for all possible market outcomes during the scheduling period, ensuring that at least one suitable scenario remains when the actual market prices and renewal status become known. This method has been tested using real data from the Australian National Electricity Market. Researchers who utilize silicon based quantum computing have a pressing need for reliable methods to generate and measure the state of qubits located in the atomic layers of silicon. Our investigation focused on mercury telluride quantum wells without a bandgap, examining how their structure influences quantum transport properties. By combining experimental measurements with theoretical analysis, we gained insight into the local distribution of states and evaluated transport characteristics through semi-empirical modeling. Our research revealed the importance of wide wells in controlling transport phenomena and demonstrated that a specific trench geometry can result in the coexistence of zero-gap and semi-Dirac behavior in adjacent regions. Additionally, wide wells were found to exhibit semi-Dirac behavior and semi-metallic characteristics alternately, depending on width. Our study also identified potential sources of scattering and estimated their influence on transport properties. Furthermore, we explored the effects of magnetic fields on transport properties and observed the emergence of mass-less, massive, and semi-Dirac spectra in the zero-field limit. Our telluride quantum wells offer a promising platform for investigating complex transport phenomena in low-dimensional, gapless materials under magnetic fields. With advancements in growth technology, it is possible to replicate the results and explore new effects in larger, more sophisticated structures. In Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD), base stations allocate dedicated time slots for multiple-model operations and data transmission. To achieve efficient resource utilization, allocating the same model to multiple bases within a small area is beneficial but is challenged by different model requirements in various locations. We introduce a new approach, Model Allocation in a Non-Cooperative Game (MA-NGC), where bases compete to allocate the most suitable model for their geographical area. By analyzing the pure Nash Equilibrium (PNE) of MA-NGC, we find that it leads to a distributed strategy allowing bases to select a model that maximizes overall utility while considering neighboring bases' models. However, since there is no standard challenge in defining a PNE from initial allocations, MA-NGC may converge to a PNE with complex models' distribution patterns. To address this issue, we propose a simple and efficient Distributed Model Allocation (DMA) protocol that guarantees a near-optimal PNE even in challenging scenarios. By simulating DMA in various networks, we demonstrate its high performance in different scenarios. Furthermore, we show that DMA is robust against different parameter variations. To validate DMA's practical feasibility, we implement DMA in our testbed and successfully test DMA on multiple networks. Finally, we explore DMA's potential applications in 5G Networks. To achieve this, we introduce new challenges and potential solutions for DMA in 5G Networks. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first challenge to define MA-NGC and the first solution to be DMA in the context of Dynamic TDD in 5G Networks. Deep neural networks can be viewed as approximations of their input functions, and their gradient behavior can provide insights into their performance. This work focuses on acquiring gradient information using Hamiltonian Neural Networks, which are modeled as neural compositions that generate responses to input signals. We explored two methods to extract gradient information: directly from the network's output or from its input. However, our primary approach involved using the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno algorithm to adjust the Hamiltonian parameters, which are analogous to backpropagation in traditional neural networks. We found that this method allows the derivation of updated Hamiltonian values, equivalent to the computation of gradients in conventional neural networks. This discovery is significant because it demonstrates that, under these conditions, the Hamiltonian NNs can be viewed as if they are computing gradients rather than outputs. This perspective is crucial for addressing the challenge of acquiring gradients in HNNs. This research also introduced several new Hamiltonian-based optimization algorithms, which can be applied to complex real-world problems. Our findings on the relationship between HNNs and gradient computation have the potential to contribute to the development of more efficient optimization algorithms based on the BFGS method and provide a starting point for further research aimed at exploring the connection between HNNs and the computation of gradients. This connection can be utilized to create more complex models based on Hamiltonian Neural Networks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghoul101/Hamiltonian-Optimization-Algorithms. Our Hamiltonian-based optimization algorithms have been tested on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, which are presented in Appendix D.2. This work is an extension of our previous conference paper titled "Hamiltonian Neural Network Optimization" presented at the 32nd Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, which focused solely on the basic BFGS algorithm. This extended version includes the derivation of the updated Hamiltonian values, new Hamiltonian-based optimization algorithms, and results from additional experiments. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT-based models, have led to significant improvements in WSD performance.  However, these models' reliance on vast amounts of data makes it difficult to prepare effective training datasets for the task.  In response to this challenge, the practice of using Context-Gloss pairs has become a standard in WSD training.  These pairs consist of a context paragraph and a word with one of its defined meanings, commonly sourced from online dictionaries.  Despite their widespread use, research shows that the current methodology may be suboptimal, as it fails to account for the available lexical knowledge, particularly in the form of dictionaries.  To address this issue, our research proposes selecting gloss definitions that are both semantically distinct and closely related to the target word, with the goal of creating more informative Context-Gloss pairs.  We demonstrate that this approach can be effective in identifying high-quality pairs that outperform randomly selected baselines.  Furthermore, we incorporate a method for modeling the relationships between different gloss definitions, which can be both similar to and distinct from the target word, in a framework called Context-Gloss Expansion.  In Context-Gloss Expansion, we generate additional definitions for each word based on these pairs, which can be used to create more comprehensive dictionaries.  Our evaluation of both individual components and the full Context-Gloss Expansion framework reveals its superiority over existing WSD approaches.  We also examine the Context-Gloss Expansion's performance in comparison to other dictionary-based WSD methods.  Our code is available online at github.com/salestock/wsd-context-gloss.  With the current proliferation of abundant lexical knowledge available online, this methodology offers a promising avenue for further research.  In particular, we explore the integration of Context-Gloss Expansion with Wikipedia-based dictionaries, which demonstrates its potential to tackle the core WSD challenge. In response to this issue, we develop a method for filtering out these noisy definitions, which in turn leads to a significant improvement in performance, thereby setting a new baseline for the task.  Our approach exceeds the performance of existing Wikipedia-based dictionaries, which were previously considered to be the best available methods for WSD. This approach extends previous work by incorporating fluctuations beyond the mean-field approximation and accounts for variations in both hydrodynamic velocities and thermodynamic properties. By combining hydrodynamic and random fluctuations within a unified framework, we derive equations that describe phase-space fluctuations in over 20 hydrodynamic velocities and thermodynamic properties. Machine learning models often benefit from tuning hyperparameters to achieve the best performance. Due to the varying nature of training and testing sets in model selection methods, researchers have proposed techniques such as k-fold cross-validation to evaluate models objectively. However, this method is prone to producing a large number of estimates, making it difficult to compare different models. A common approach to compare models is to calculate their average performance based on multiple repetitions of the experiment. Unfortunately, this approach ignores the source of variance associated with the model itself, which can lead to incorrect conclusions about the performance of different models. This issue is particularly problematic when selecting the optimal number of folds in k-fold cross-validation, as it is challenging to determine if the observed differences between models are genuine or a result of sampling. In this paper, we propose using the variance component of the k-fold cross-validation estimator in conjunction with the mean performance to guide model selection. We demonstrate that this approach not only accounts for the sampling variance but also provides a more accurate comparison of models. Furthermore, we derive the variance component of the leave-one-out cross-validation estimator, which can be used to compare models with a focus on model validation. In addition, we discuss the relationship between the proposed method and other model selection techniques, including Bayesian approaches. To validate our proposed method, we conducted a series of experiments using both synthetic and real-world data. Our results indicate that our method performs optimally in comparison to other established techniques of model selection. Our proposed approach is suitable for a wide range of machine learning applications, including natural language processing, deep learning, and others. The fabric space of a metric graph represents the set of all possible flat embeddings in the Euclidean plane. Given two metric graphs with distinct topological properties, we demonstrate that their fabric spaces inevitably differ topologically. Furthermore, this distinction extends to their associated random walk models, leading to a distinction in the walk's solvability. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on accurate organ modeling, but modeling soft tissues as non-rigid volumes rather than surfaces offers advantages in navigation, imaging, and surgical planning.  However, aligning preoperative volume data to intraoperative surface registration remains a challenging task due to the complexity of biomechanical models and the limited number of corresponding points between volumes and surfaces.  We present a novel non-rigid volume-to-surface alignment approach that leverages a simplified biomechanical model combining diffusion and fluid dynamics.  By solving the partial differential equations numerically, we employ a finite element method to model tissue deformation, utilizing a small set of corresponding points to inform the solution.  The method is computationally efficient, allowing for real-time performance on modern graphics processing units.  We evaluate our method on 23 datasets from different abdominal organ surgeries and compare it to a state-of-the-art machine learning-based approach, demonstrating superior performance in terms of alignment accuracy.  The method has been applied in clinical practice with satisfactory results.  The algorithm is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghassen89/Vol2Surf-Alignment.  The datasets used in this study are available for research purposes upon request.  The method has been validated by experienced surgeons in three separate laparoscopic surgeries.  The algorithm has been designed to accommodate different biomechanical models, enabling researchers to easily exchange models with minimal modification to the framework.  The framework has been developed using Python, with the help of the PyVisca package for graphics processing unit acceleration.  The code for the finite element method has been developed in-house, with the option to use the PyFR package. However, this process is associated with the emergence of pullers that smooth out the system, contradicting our initial expectation of roughening.  To resolve this issue, the researchers changed their perspective to look for processes associated with the formation of pullers that promote erosion rather than smoothing. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases often relies on a small number of highly infectious super-spreaders whose occasional appearance can significantly contribute to epidemic outbreaks. This paper provides a mathematical model to analyze how occurrences of super-spreaders affect the course of an epidemic. A key feature of our model is the assumption that super-spreaders appear infrequently at random times, forming an Poisson process that can be both time-dependent and variable across different individuals. Using this model, we calculated the expected number of super-spreaders that emerge within a given time frame, both in terms of time since the start of the epidemic and in terms of the individual's susceptibility to it. Furthermore, we derived equations to model the early stages of the epidemic, finding that it can be divided into either a phase where the super-spreaders dominate the transmission of the disease or a phase where the epidemic enters a self-sustaining cycle of transmission. In the former case, the model reveals an exponential relationship between the initial size of the super-spreaders' group and the resulting outbreak size. In the latter case, the model shows that small super-spreaders can have a major impact on the epidemic's outcome, with certain configurations even leading to an inevitably disastrous outcome for the epidemic. In addition to this analysis, we also examined a more general model that removes the restriction on a fixed group size during the early stages of the epidemic, finding that it can also exhibit an inevitable disastrous outcome due to the presence of super-spreaders. This research was inspired by the high transmission rate of COVID-19 and specifically examined the occurrence of super-spreaders at conferences and in airliner flights. The calculated data were then compared to real-world data for these situations, revealing that the model can accurately capture the underlying dynamics of these events. This finding suggests that similar models could be applied to other outbreaks of this type, providing valuable insights that could be used to mitigate their transmission. Accurate measurements of solar vector magnetic fields are crucial for understanding the behavior of magnetic fields in the sun. The development of advanced inversion techniques has led to multiple algorithms deriving equivalent photospheric quantities that can determine magnetic fields, with various methods proposed to combine these derived variables effectively. Nonetheless, incorporating these multiple solutions can be challenging due to their disparate mathematical formulations, often involving a variety of biased and scaled solutions with unclear sources of bias, which hinders their direct combination. This problem is particularly evident when employing the most straightforward method, using a fully connected network, due to its symmetry. To address this issue, a non-orthogonal angle network was proposed, which breaks the symmetry and consistently determines the necessary signs. When applied to a simple example from chemistry, this method demonstrated the complex network's ability to accurately replicate the correct signs after just 7 parameters had been learned. When using a more realistic Hamiltonian matrix from physics, the method successfully identified the correct signs following the training of 400 parameters. To further investigate this model's capabilities, a simplified variant was created, and by analyzing the learned parameters, it became clear that the model is capable of effectively learning the Hamiltonian's signs with a compact set of 25 parameters. To expand the model's applications, a general framework was suggested that enables the use of complex networks for any discrete transformation by first determining the necessary basis states and then defining the desired transformation as the projection onto those states. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method known as ReCross, which employs prior model predictions to target related samples within a vast dataset, fine-tuning the model on these selected examples to achieve state-of-the-art performance in various evaluation metrics.
Our proposed method effectively distills implicit knowledge from existing data, thereby boosting the models' effectiveness in various tasks and demonstrating substantial improvements over baseline methods. Moreover, ReCross showcases versatile applications, with the potential to engage simple language models in complex tasks, combine the strengths of diverse models, and even counter the issue of model drift. By sharing our method with the community, we are excited to provide ReCross as a pre-trained model to facilitate further exploration and valuable insights for cross-task generalization. A systematic search for planetary nebulae within the Fornax cluster cluster region yielded nearly 1200 confirmed objects, with nearly 900 assigned to galaxies and the remainder classified as foreground or background nebulae. This study employs a custom nebular code to model planetary nebulae spectra and mitigate free-free emission distortion, further adapted to match the Hubble Space Telescope photometry of 24 known planetary nebulae satellites within the galaxy NGC 1316. By analyzing the [OIII] lambda 5000 Å line, researchers distinguished between nebular and stellar components in the spectral data, with the addition of photometric constraints for extragalactic planetary nebulae. A comparative analysis with previously determined distances showed that the planetary nebulae method produces comparable results, with some exceptions. Ultimately, this study establishes a planetary nebula-based luminosity distance of 19.6 megaparsecs with a margin of error, utilizing the standard globular cluster abundance pattern within the Fornax cluster galaxies. Additionally, researchers found a median central black hole mass of less than 10 to the power of 5 solar masses in the galaxies of the Fornax cluster. A super stellar mass density threshold of roughly 10 to the power of 8.8 solar masses per cubic parsec is implied by this finding. Further investigation is necessary to confirm the implications of this result. The comprehensive planetary nebula database compiled in this study is now publicly accessible. The research underlying this study was conducted as part of the Fornax3D observational initiative. Processing temporal data streams efficiently is a pressing challenge for various applications including database management systems. Stream processing engines like Apache Flink and Apache Spark Streaming have high overheads due to their robust nature, making them unsuitable for numerous scenarios. We present a new stream processing engine, LifeFlow, optimized for continuous queries over static datasets and small, slowly changing input streams. By leveraging memory-based window processing and efficient index structures, LifeFlow achieves substantial performance gains. For benchmark tests using small datasets with low update rates, LifeFlow outperforms Apache Flink by a factor of up to 15 and Spark Streaming by a factor of up to 20. Furthermore, LifeFlow demonstrates high efficiency in Flink SQL evaluations, surpassing Flink by a factor of up to 5 when executing SQL queries over static datasets. We also provide detailed implementation particulars of LifeFlow's core components including its window and index structures, as well as a discussion on various optimization strategies used to enhance performance. Experimental evaluations of LifeFlow against Apache Flink show that its performance gains can be attributed to both its streamlined design and the efficiency of its window and index structures. We also examine LifeFlow's scalability in large-scale input stream settings, discovering that it scales linearly with available CPU resources. Ultimately, LifeFlow's compact and efficient design positions it as a high-performance choice for managing small, slowly changing input data streams. We provide the source code for LifeFlow freely on GitHub under the Apache License 2.0.

Traditional coherent CPM detection requires knowledge of the carrier phase and often incorporates differential processing to achieve coherence. This method can be coherent, semi-coherent, or non-coherent, with non-coherent detection being the most resilient to channel instability. However, it generally suffers from carrier phase uncertainty, which can be mitigated by an expanded delay of the differential detection signal. This paper explores the concept of delayed differential detection in CPM. It begins by reviewing the basics of CPM modulation, followed by an examination of its non-coherent detection methods. We then derive an expression for the generalized delay of CPM signals based on their frequency response properties. Specifically, we determine the optimal delay for three well-known CPM types: MSK, GMSK, and MINSK. It is demonstrated that this optimal delay can be obtained directly from the frequency response spectra of these signals. Furthermore, we provide a derivate for the delay of MSK and GMSK signals in the narrowband case. Lastly, we offer numerical data on the delay for additional CPM signals, including Gaussian Filtered Baseband CPM and MINSK with multiple-order memory. These results can be utilized to identify whether the delay of a CPM signal is sufficiently large, thus enabling it to employ non-coherent differential detection with reduced performance degradation. This in turn facilitates better system design and performance optimization. It is worth noting that the delay expressed in symbol durations is typically quite lengthy, ranging from 10 to 100 or more, which can be misleading due to its dimensional nature. This conversion is both necessary and useful, as it provides a more accurate and meaningful interpretation of the delay in bits. This formula can be further simplified to $d_b = \lfloor (N_c-1) \rfloor + 1$, where $N_c$ is the signal's cycle length. To improve speech recognition, it's suggested that the connection between speech and text be strengthened by training them together. This approach splits the training process into two parts: first, the speech model is fine-tuned using transcriptions, and then the text model is fine-tuned using audio recordings. We propose a more unified approach, dubbed bidirectional focus, in which the models are combined and trained to minimize the gap between their individual contributions. In this framework, the speech model is trained to accurately predict corresponding text transcripts, and the text model is trained to predict associated audio recordings. As a result, the models develop a deeper understanding of each other, leading to a 10.7% improvement in the correct transcription of WER rates for our testing dataset. Furthermore, this approach allows for the derivation of a simple residual training method, which can be applied to existing speech recognition systems for a 5.6% WER reduction. The code for this project is available online at github.com/ParandDarabi/speech-text-modal.

Coreference resolution is the task of identifying relationships of equivalence between phrases in a text, with the goal of resolving multiple references to the same entity into a single representative.  Despite the progress made by neural networks in coreference resolution, the underlying principles of this process are not well understood.  This work delves into the fundamentals of coreference resolution, examining the relationship between the tokens that serve as references to the same entity and those that do not.  With the development of a suitable metric, it is possible to quantify this relationship as the difference between the probability of two tokens being references to the same entity, given that they refer to the same entity, and one being a reference to the other.  This ratio has been applied to multiple datasets across various languages, revealing that the proportion of the tokens that refer to each other is consistently less than one, often near 0.2.  This phenomenon can be seen as the "centering" effect, where the texts prefer to reference the same entity with different phrases rather than using the same phrase.  By taking this ratio into account, it was possible to integrate a crucial feature into the coreference resolution network, significantly improving its performance.  This work also offers a straightforward strategy for evaluating the network's performance at multiple thresholds, in addition to the development of a straightforward metric that can be applied to neural networks through the derivation of a suitable probability distribution.  Furthermore, it is possible to integrate this feature into a pre-trained network via few-shot learning, in a setting with limited data.  A simple approach to doing so is proposed. The metric dimension of a graph measures the minimum number of markers required to uniquely identify vertices within the graph based on their distance characteristics to those markers. We introduce the concept of partial labels, which can be assigned to vertices to dimension the graph, and define the shortened metric dimension of a graph as the minimum number of markers needed to assign partial labels to vertices in a way that accurately identifies all vertices. We examine the relationship between the standard metric dimension and its shortened counterpart, establishing that the former exceeds the latter in size. We also determine the shortened metric dimension of several specific graph types and provide bounds on its size for general graphs, ultimately leading to the conclusion that the shortened metric dimension can potentially exceed the standard metric dimension by more than just one unit. Moreover, we contribute feasible algorithms for determining both the standard and shortened metric dimensions of particular graph types. Lastly, we offer a distinguished vertex version of the shortened metric dimension and investigate its properties in relation to existing measures. Open problems are presented to further advance the field. This study is an extended version of a previous work that has been published. The original research appeared in the proceedings of the 12th International Conference on colored (distributed) algorithms, data structures and architectures, and communication networks, 2020. The original work by its authors was funded by the National Science Foundation under grant IIS-1828081. In a sequence of independent decisions made by independent agents, where each agent makes one decision, if the first agent in a fixed order has high-quality preferences and makes an informed choice, it can lead to a high-quality outcome for all agents, even if there are many of them. This is true regardless of the distribution of agents' individual interests. This paper explores how adding more agents with private interests in a serial dictatorship scenario affects the outcome when some agents always act in their own self-interest. It also examines how a mechanism that selects the first agent based on a performance-related criterion can lead to high-quality outcomes for all, as well as more equitable distribution of benefits when interests are diverse. Furthermore, it is possible to design a simple and efficient way to determine outcomes in situations involving many agents with individual interests. Lastly, it is demonstrated that this approach can be applied to complex, dynamic environmental problems. If the choices made by the first agent in a fixed order are of high quality, it can also be inferred that it is beneficial to give more authority to the upper levels of a hierarchy rather than the lower levels.
