We investigated nearly 1.2 million asteroids discovered by Pan-STARRS1, focusing on its binary population and identifying potential pairs. By analyzing the positions and magnitudes of asteroids across multiple images, we developed an algorithm to detect binaries. We accounted for variations in magnitudes due to orbital periods and eccentricities, establishing a threshold to distinguish binary systems from coincidental alignments of nearby asteroids. Approximately 1.5% of the studied asteroids appear to be binary systems, with masses ranging from 10 to 600 kilometers in diameter. We found that small binaries (less than 100 kilometers in diameter) predominate, with only a few exceptions of larger systems. Compared to the overall population, binaries with high eccentricities are more common among asteroids in the inner solar system. We also observed a similar binary eccentricity distribution in the outer solar system but required a larger sample to confirm this trend. Estimates suggest there are approximately 200,000 binary asteroids in our data, with masses likely representative of the solar system's total binary mass. We discuss the limitations of this analysis and potential sources of error, also examining the influence of solar insolation on binary formation and survival. While this study cannot directly determine the binary fraction, it does provide insights into the solar insolation threshold required for binary maintenance and suggests that most small bodies in the outer solar system have sufficient mass to remain stable despite tidal forces. Furthermore, we found evidence for binary formation among smaller asteroids in the outer solar system, and discuss possible methods for confirming this finding, including analyzing high-eccentricity binaries and examining the distribution of binary orbits. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for exploring binary asteroids in deeper surveys. For our analysis, we developed publicly available software called BAaD, utilizing Python libraries including scipy, numpy, pandas, and scipy-optimize. BAaD can be applied to binary asteroid detection across various surveys, as well as other projects involving data analysis for overlapping sources. We intend for BAaD to be a starting point for further optimization and enhancements, including integrating it with more advanced optimization techniques, incorporating priors based on asteroid orbital elements, and adapting it for real-time applications on large datasets. Ultimately, BAaD offers a foundational framework for investigating binary asteroids across various surveys and datasets. For our purposes, we used a simple model to calculate the parallax of binary systems, also deriving an expression for its relationship with eccentricity. We found that the distribution of binary systems is influenced by solar insolation, with most surviving at an orbital distance of 2.5

This study examines a linear regression model where one of the variables has a linear relationship, and the remaining variables follow a logistic form. We derive an estimator for the coefficients of this partially linear model and establish its asymptotic properties. To extend this model to accommodate network data, we substitute peer influence variables for some of the covariates. We then investigate the consistency of our estimator in both fixed-g and growing-network designs. Additionally, we discuss the challenges and limitations of this model when applied to network data, including issues of sparsity and endogeneity. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the performance of our estimator. We also briefly discuss the model's potential extensions and its relationship to existing literature. A companion paper explores the model's empirical applications to educational peer effects using a network dataset. A note on terminology: we use the term "logistic regression" to refer to the logistic form model, even when the dependent variable is not binary. This form can be seen as a special case of generalized linear models with a log-link function and a gamma distribution. However, due to the prevalence of this terminology in the literature, we use "logistic regression" throughout this paper. Similarly, we use the term "linear regression" to refer to linear models, even when the dependent variable is not continuous. A more appropriate term in this context would be "linear location-science model." A note on notation: we use bold lowercase letters to denote vectors, with the exception of the dependent variable $y_i$ and the response variable $r_i$. We use uppercase bold letters to denote matrices, with the exception of $\boldsymbol{0}$ and $\boldsymbol{I}$. We use standard notation for other mathematical objects. A note on style: we follow the style guidelines of the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B. A note on software: we provide the R code for the numerical examples in the supplementary materials. A note on replication: we replicate the results in the companion paper using a network dataset from the National Longitudinal Study of Youth (NLSY). A note on related work: we discuss the relationship between our model and existing literature in the discussion section. A note on acknowledgments: we acknowledge the support of the National Science Foundation via grant DMS-1710090. We also acknowledge the support of the Harvard Center for Research on Network Effects via grant HAR-2019-LD-101. In our research, we created and tested a framework for guiding artificial intelligence dungeon masters through Dungeons and Dragons adventures using a specific technique. This method involves assigning a particular mindset to the DM, which is reflected in their decision-making process and storytelling style. Our aim was to explore if this approach could lead to more engaging and relevant storylines for players. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we designed a laboratory test in which a lone DM navigated a pre-existing adventure using our framework. The resulting experience was compared to a control group composed of traditional D&D parties playing the same adventure. Our findings suggest that the framework leads to more exciting and coherent stories, which also better suit the players' individual preferences. Furthermore, by analyzing the dialogue between the DM and players, we gained insight into the challenges of creating a natural language interface for directing a DM, and the importance of considering the social aspects of the D&D experience. Our research has implications for the development of artificial intelligence dungeon masters and provides a foundation for further study into the complex dynamics of D&D parties. Our pre-compiled D&D dataset is available for public use. The code underlying our research is also openly accessible. The findings from our laboratory test have been compiled into a comprehensive report, which is included in the supplementary materials. The paper presented is a condensed version of the original submission to the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, and it includes additional context, a more detailed explanation of our methodology, as well as the results from our subsequent evaluation of the framework in a real-world setting. The appendix to the paper is comprised of three main sections: the first section describes the design of our laboratory test, including the modifications made to the pre-existing D&D adventure and the methodology used to evaluate the effectiveness of the framework; the second section delves into the challenges encountered during the development of the AI DM supervisor's handbook, with a particular focus on the issues related to directing the DM through natural language; the third and final section explores the possibilities for generalizing the framework to other types of interactive storytelling. Recent advancements in natural language processing have prioritized the development of models that can generate high-quality, realistic counterfactuals, especially in areas like conversational dialogue. However, such efforts tend to focus on individual words or simple statements rather than entire phrases of varying complexity. To address this gap, we introduce a new counterfactual generation task called phrasal counterfactual extraction, where given a context and a relevant sentence, the objective is to create a counterfactual version of one or more specified phrases within the sentence while maintaining semantic consistency. We've established a set of rules to evaluate this task, which includes assessing the counterfactual phrase's semantic relationship with both its original counterpart and the intended meaning of the original sentence. We've also created two datasets, one for training and a more challenging one for testing, and have explored various methods to demonstrate the feasibility of this task. Our results show that fine-tuning natural language generation models using a suitable loss function can effectively handle this challenge. We've made our datasets and implementation available for further research. This task has implications for areas like conversational dialogue, where counterfactual statements about previously discussed topics could be generated, and we outline potential avenues for exploration. Multilabel classification problems involve categorizing data points into any number of given categories, with many real-world applications such as content categorization, user profiling, and genetic annotation. Standard supervised multilabel learning methods train models on perfectly annotated data, but in many cases, we must work with incomplete labels, as it is common for only one positive class to be indicated per instance. However, in many real-world scenarios, this partial annotation significantly reduces the effectiveness of standard multilabel models. This paper addresses this issue by developing a method to accurately predict multilabel instances from partially annotated data by utilizing just one marked positive class. We provide comprehensive experimental evidence showing that this approach leads to substantial performance gains when working with datasets annotated in this subpar manner. Furthermore, we introduce a simple yet effective way to enhance performance in cases where more complete annotations are available. This research also involves collaborating with experts in the field of molecular biology to accurately annotate and analyze a particular dataset. The resulting technique has been named Multilabel Instance Extraction, or MIE. The code for this project is publicly accessible.

In contrast, we concentrate on short-circuiting the inverse problem, aiming to create a highly expedient compressor that can rapidly compact fluid dynamics data. Reinforcement learning models for dialogue often rely on artificially
constructed datasets as evaluation metrics. Currently, there is no widely
accepted method to assess dialogue models in a dynamic real-world setting.
In this work, we introduce a cutting-edge framework, L2Explorer, to
systematically explore how user interactions evolve over time in response to
changing preferences within a hypothetical online dating website domain.
Similar to showcasting, our interactive evaluation environment showcases
the complexities of real-world user interactions under the influence of
dynamic preferences. However, unlike existing approaches, L2Explorer enables
the evaluation of dialogue models across infinite sessions with unique user
profiles by utilizing infinite, statistically-generated user profile datasets.
To demonstrate the efficacy of L2Explorer, we utilize it to evaluate a
state-of-the-art dialogue model on the multi-turn movie recommendation task.
The resulting performance metrics over endless, artificially-generated
scenarios reveal that simple transformer-based dialogue models excel compared
to sophisticated memory-based alternatives. The L2Explorer framework is
open-sourced at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/L2Explorer.

When $X$ is affine and the action is defined by regular functions, we can employ elimination theory to demonstrate the equivalence of these compactifications. Furthermore, we show that for a hypersurface defined by a polynomial with coefficients as variables, the compactifications associated with the zero set of that polynomial are equivalent to the compactifications obtained through the use of an associated homogeneous polynomial. Lastly, we provide specific examples related to the action of $G_m$ on $\mathbb{A}^1$, demonstrating how this framework can be applied to those situations.

By incorporating contributions from bulges and disks in the total stellar mass, we find that the turnover mass in giant galaxies is approximately 5.5 times 10 to the 10th power solar masses, with minimal variation across different galaxy metallicity levels. Furthermore, by integrating observations of low-mass galaxies with bulge components, we demonstrate that the turnover mass can be accurately predicted as the mass at which the bulge-to-total light ratio equals one-half, exceeding 10 to the 10th power solar masses for bulge-dominated galaxies similar to our own. Existing theoretical bulge formation scenarios fail to effectively explain the extent of the turnover, suggesting that it must be influenced by additional factors that disrupt bulge growth, allowing the transition to thin disk systems to proceed, and thus, the M*-SFR connection continues to shift to higher masses with cosmic time. This paper focuses on a common issue in XLA, specifically the varied nature of sentiment words' meanings across different languages. To address this challenge, we developed a multi-task learning framework for CLSA, incorporating two primary tasks: (1) sentiment classification and (2) word semantic translation. This approach learns distinct representations for a given word's sentiment and its core meaning across different languages. We demonstrated the value of our approach through experiments on three datasets. Our results showed that the proposed method outperforms the competition in multiple settings. Furthermore, we discovered a noteworthy phenomenon where incorporating a related, but different language does not necessarily contribute to a better CLSA performance due to the presence of noisy data. To mitigate this issue, we developed a strategy to only incorporate relevant languages. Our findings are consistent across two specific datasets. We also examined the performance of our approach using a more comprehensive dataset, consisting of 14 languages. Our results remained superior even when comparing the multi-task learning approach to a carefully curated selection of the competition. Finally, we explored the practical applications of our method to a limited extent. However, we believe there are numerous unexplored opportunities waiting to be discovered. Our code is available online at github.com/sunshine1999/CSA-NET. Moreover, we created a publicly accessible CLSA dataset for the English and Chinese languages, available at this link: https://github.com/sunshine1999/CLSA-DCFC/wiki. Lastly, we invite interested researchers to join our ongoing discussion forum at the following URL: https://github.com/sunshine1999/CSA-NET/discussions.

Recently published research indicates that solar proton events can be confused with neutron events due to the limited sensitivity of some space-borne detectors to neutrons. As a result, many neutron events are likely misclassified as proton events. To address this challenge, scientists have developed methods to differentiate between neutrons and protons based on their distinct energies and the effects they have on space-borne electronics aboard satellites. By applying these distinctions to data from the MIPOT detector, which is sensitive to both protons and neutrons, researchers have re-examined previous solar proton measurements, particularly during the intense event that occurred on November 7, 2004. Re-classifying the neutrons as protons has significantly increased the estimated solar proton flux for this event by a factor of approximately ten, with peak energies reaching over 1 GeV. Furthermore, the extended duration of this event is also revealed, indicating that large solar flares can sometimes result in extensive high-energy proton storms lasting several days. The refined analysis highlights the importance of accurately distinguishing between neutrons and protons to gain a more precise understanding of solar flares and their effects on space-borne electronics. The findings associated with this specific event may have implications for satellite reliability assessments within the solar maximum segment. The re-classified data are available through the virtual solar flare museum portal. The associated code is publicly accessible via GitHub. The updated solar proton data with associated errors are provided in the appendix. The code used for neutron proton differentiation can also be used for other space-borne detectors with similar neutron proton sensitivity. The research was supported by NASA's Heliophysics Division. A significant issue in using deep learning for medical imaging is the presence of contraindicative pathologic tissue. This challenge can be applied to MRI data containing lesions such as brain abscesss, tumors, or strokes. In order to develop a robust and universal pre-processing technique for removing such lesions from MRI data, a variational auto-encoder network was proposed. This encoder translates MRI scans without lesions into latent feature spaces, while producing complementary encoded images with corresponding lesion-filled overlays in the spatial domain. Encoded images without lesions can be obtained through decoding of these features. Encoded images with lesions were also incorporated into a 3D UNet-based segmentation framework, resulting in enhanced performance in comparing encoded/decoded pairs. Moreover, this framework's ability to generate graded lesions was utilized, enabling the creation of highly realistic training datasets with varied lesion types and degrees. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become truly entangled with the others if its cavity is highly anti-orthogonal to another cavity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this unconnected system can serve as a central node in a cluster state protocol, generating entanglement between previously unconnected parties. Lastly, we explore the feasibility of achieving high levels of anti-orthogonality experimentally. If achievable, this could enable the creation of truly entangled states between unconnected atomic systems via Jaynes-Cummings interactions.

As computer systems and software become increasingly complex, maintaining their reliability and performance requires more time and resources. To manage this challenge, developers often restrict or approximate parts of their systems to achieve faster development and deployment. However, these changes can have unintended consequences, causing issues to appear in previously tested or known areas of the system. To address this problem, we introduce Decanter, a tool that helps developers identify decoupling issues that may arise from these scale-oriented approximations. Decanter takes as input approximate and original system descriptions and uses a combination of model-checking and scale-oriented mining techniques to detect differences in how the system behaves at different scales. We evaluated Decanter on three real-world case studies involving approximate deep learning models, nested network communications, and concurrent multi-threaded programs. These experiments showed that Decanter effectively pinpoints decoupling issues that may arise from these approximations and highlights opportunities to further develop Decanter and similar tools to further integrate its features with existing system development methodologies. Decanter and its methodology are available open-source on GitHub. This research also led to a broader decoupling theory, which we call Restricted Effectiveness, and a corresponding methodology, providing a framework for validating the effectiveness of scale-oriented approximations. This framework includes a set of guidelines that developers can use to ensure their approximations remain effective and do not lead to unforeseen consequences. We believe this framework and its methodology can be applied to a wide range of scale-oriented approximations across various areas of computer science. This research started as a technical debt management project for the Apache Flink project, which led to a broader decoupling theory and a corresponding validation methodology for scale-oriented approximations. This experience and the resulting validation methodology have been continuously integrated into Flink's development process. This research received no external funding. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/decoupling/decanter. This research was conducted without the involvement of an institution. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's impact factor is investigated, and it is demonstrated that non-abelian effects from small-x BFKL calculations are required to correctly interpret data in terms of this distribution. However, determining the TMD gluon distribution's access through the color dipole gluon distribution introduces an additional challenge related to the impact factor's Borel integrand, which includes both non-perturbative contributions related to infrared renormalons and nonperturbative effects from hadronization. To address this issue, we develop a method that removes the renormalon-related components from the impact factor's Borel integrand. It is shown that even in the presence of nonperturbative hadronization effects, the TMD gluon distribution can be accessed through a dispersive integral along the complex plane, which only involves the impact factor's Borel transform for an initial complex $b$-value. The characteristics of this initial $b$-value determine the complex $b$-value for the integral, which in turn influences the TMD gluon distribution's access. Even though the Borel transform for an initial complex $b$-value contains renormalon-related nonperturbative components, these components become negligible as the impact factor's order increases, as observed in both the BFKL and saturation approaches. Consequently, the impact factor's Borel transform for an initial complex $b$-value is expected to be reliable for deep saturation protons, and the proposed method's applicability is validated through comparisons with either the BFKL or saturation approaches for proton fragmentation. The proposed method is further applied to investigate the impact of infrared renormalons on the color dipole gluon distribution's access, and it is demonstrated that the nonperturbative hadronization effects from the impact factor's Borel integrand are removed through a suitable choice of complex $b$-value. The removed components are replaced by the dispersion integral along the complex plane, which involves the impact factor's Borel transform for this chosen complex $b$-value. Even though the nonperturbative hadronization effects from the impact factor's Borel integrand are removed, the complex $b$-value's characteristics remain, which determine the dispersion integral along the complex plane, and it is found that this complex $b$-value is directly related to the nonperturbative hadronization effects on the impact factor. Many real-world situations involve adapting models to new, unseen data without access to the original training set. This challenge is particularly relevant for various security-sensitive applications, including but not limited limited to, classification systems within operating systems and machine learning-based safety critical software.  In such contexts, where model sharing is impossible, researchers have explored methods for transferring knowledge from a trained model via a black-box framework based solely on the model's decision-making outputs. However, the effectiveness of these techniques is generally task-specific and fail to generalize to new, unanticipated data. In this work, we propose a novel, one-time off-line approach to prepare a generic, universally applicable model that can facilitate zero-shot knowledge transfer across a broad spectrum of tasks and domains.  Unlike previous methods, this framework leverages the model's predictive probabilities instead of classification outputs to achieve generalizability.  By utilizing a pre-trained model to generate problem-specific training data for any given task, we demonstrate that knowledge transfer is possible across diverse domains with varying levels of similarity.  Furthermore, this approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in several benchmark scenarios, including but not limited to, simple and complex scenarios with both similar and different domain relationships.  The proposed framework also scales to large-scale real-world scenarios, as evident from its successful application to the Wikipedia article categorization problem.  This achievement is made possible by the proposed framework's ability to utilize a limited amount of existing data to achieve zero-shot knowledge transfer in a broad range of contexts.  The code for this work is available at https://github.com/omar-al-khodairy/Generalized-Domain-Adapation.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct the lattice from its peak operators, there is still no straightforward algorithm to automatically generate lattices from this approach. In certain cases, particularly when working with modules over the integer lattice, submodules can be found using computational tools. However, even with these methods, determining all submodules of a module is not always feasible. In such situations, researchers often resort to constructing the lattice of submodules of a module that contains the module of interest as a submodule. This approach allows them to include additional submodules in the lattice, which can provide a more accurate and complete picture. In the context of integer lattices, modules that are multiplicity-free offer another advantage. In such cases, the lattice of submodules can be constructed using the irreducible modules as building blocks, which greatly simplifies the construction process. Nonetheless, even with multiplicity-free modules, determining the irreducible modules is not always a straightforward task and often requires additional information. In the paper discussed here, we present a method for constructing the lattice of submodules of a multiplicity-free module using only limited information. This method involves analyzing the decomposition matrices of the module in question and its extension to obtain the irreducible modules and their corresponding multiplicities. Once this information is obtained, the lattice of submodules can be constructed using the method proposed by Stanley. The paper also includes three examples that demonstrate this method at work. The first example involves determining the lattice of submodules of the module $R(2,1)$, the second example concerns the module $R(3,3)$, and the third example is more complex and involves the module $R(4,2)$. The proposed method can be applied to modules over the integer lattice, finite fields, and certain specific modules, among others. The method proposed here for constructing the lattice of submodules of a multiplicity-free module can also be applied to modules that are not multiplicity-free by removing the redundant modules from the lattice. Despite significant progress in reinforcement learning, co-observation scenarios where agents with different specialties collaborate and observe each other's actions present a challenge. By co-observing, agents can glean insights from each other's expertise, but their actions have contrasting purposes. This diversity makes their observation purpose ambiguous, hindering the effectiveness of current methods. To address this issue, a novel framework called Cozob is proposed, combining a module that contrasts the observation purposes of different specialties and a module that guides the agent's observations based on its task specifications. By incorporating a rich representation of observation purposes, an appropriate observation space can be identified, and the agent can learn from demonstrations that are not necessarily specialized. Experimental results on complex, co-observation scenarios, including a simulated game of hide-and-seek, demonstrate the effectiveness of Cozob. The code for Cozob is available at https://github.com/ghulkin Cozob was developed at the University of Alberta.

This paper introduces two types of metrics - the average computation time per codeword ($\AC$) and the average codeword measurement time ($\AM$), which are relevant to the implementation of PAC codes. We show that codewords with a high $\AC$ are likely to have difficulty being inverted and suggest using the reciprocal of $\AC$ as a weighting factor in code design. Additionally, we explore methods for efficiently computing the inverse of PAC codes. Specifically, for codes with a single codeword, we propose a straightforward inversion process. For codes with multiple codewords, we investigate the challenge of precisely defining the set of all possible inversion scenarios. To overcome this obstacle, we employ a statistical approach by treating the codewords as random variables. As such, our research focuses on codes with randomly distributed codewords. We calculate the probability distribution of a single codeword inversion time and leverage this information to evaluate the average time it takes to compute a codeword. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the distribution of a single codeword and the distribution of all codewords, which allows us to derive the average measurement time. Our analysis incorporates both the exponential and Rayleigh distributions as codeword density models. Our research also delves into the exploration of the relationship between the codeword inversion time and the frequency content of a signal. We propose a codeword design based on the signal's spectral characteristics and the codeword-inversion time distribution. Our results demonstrate that codes with a uniform codeword distribution outperform those with a non-uniform distribution. Our research further explores the challenge of inversing codes when the available information includes only measured data. In such cases, we propose a method for deriving the codeword that is implicit in the measurement data. Our approach involves the use of a least-squares solver and the development of an algorithm that efficiently computes the inverse of a set of measured data. Our research provides numerical results that compare the performance of different codeword distributions with both simulated and real data. Our findings indicate that the proposed codeword-design algorithm yields an approximately 50% reduction in computation time when compared to a random codeword distribution. Our analysis also reveals that the proposed algorithm achieves a 20% to 30% reduction in computation time when compared to a uniform codeword distribution. Using reinforcement learning to train neural machine translation models has shown great potential, but its widespread use is limited due to the large action space involved. Typically, a model is trained on a small subset of possible target words before selecting the best one, but this method doesn't effectively utilize the full action space. We propose the encoded latent action space model, which represents the action space with a latent variable that can be efficiently searched. This allows for the use of a large action space without incurring search costs. Additionally, we introduce a technique for scaling the model by multi-agent reinforcement learning, which enables the model to learn from longer sequences by collaborating with multiple agents. Our approach outperforms existing methods on widely used machine translation datasets, including the widely used WMT English to German dataset. Code available at github.com/THU-CLG/REALT. We have examined a qubit that is part of a three-state system in a non-equilibrium steady state, driven by periodic energy supply and waste removal. The theoretical model, with small dissipation, reveals complex dynamics including periodic changes in energy and spontaneous loss of drive-matching signal. Experimentally, using periodic application of electromagnetic fields to a diamond spin, we found non-equilibrium steady states for both weak and strong driving. In the weak driving case, energy oscillation magnitude matches theoretical predictions. However, when driving is strong, energy oscillation is reduced due to thermal effects and backaction. The experimental and theoretical non-equilibrium heat rates also match when driving is weak but differ when driving is strong. The main discrepancy between theory and experiment in the strong driving case remains unclear and requires further investigation. The research demonstrates the importance of considering system initial conditions when interpreting non-equilibrium state data. We explore several evolving biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space and apply a specific operator to these hypersurfaces in order to derive relevant equations that these hypersurfaces must satisfy. Depending on whether we apply the Lorentz harmonic or minimal operator to these hypersurfaces, we derive different equation types that these hypersurfaces must satisfy. If we apply the Lorentz harmonic operator, we derive an equation involving the Ricci curvature tensor of these hypersurfaces. If we apply the minimal operator, we derive an equation involving the Ricci curvature tensor of these hypersurfaces and the Laplacian of the mean curvature of these hypersurfaces. Notably, we identify specific biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space that satisfy these derived equation types. Additionally, we provide specific conditions under which we can determine whether these hypersurfaces are minimal or not. If these hypersurfaces are not minimal, we can determine the mean curvature of these hypersurfaces and its relationship to its components. If these hypersurfaces are not minimal in three-dimensional Euclidean space, we can determine the mean curvature of these hypersurfaces and its relationship to its components and the Ricci curvature tensor of these hypersurfaces. If we apply the minimal operator to these hypersurfaces in three-dimensional Euclidean space, we derive an equation involving the Laplacian of the mean curvature of these hypersurfaces, the Ricci curvature tensor of these hypersurfaces, and the components of these hypersurfaces. Notably, we identify specific biharmonic hypersurfaces in three-dimensional Euclidean space that satisfy this derived equation type. Furthermore, we provide a numerical method for approximating the mean curvature of these hypersurfaces in two-dimensional Euclidean space. Lastly, we provide several applications related to these evolving biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space.

Given a set of fractions p/q, a non-negative integer array A is considered identifiable if the sum of the terms corresponding to numerator p of each fraction can be determined solely from the sum of the terms corresponding to the denominator q of each fraction. In other terms, knowing the values S_p and S_q allows us to exactly calculate S_n. In this study, we begin by examining the characteristics required for a set of fractions to be capable of identifying non-negative integer arrays. It is demonstrated that a set of fractions with both prime numerator and denominator components can identify any array, whereas a set with only prime numerator components can only determine the sum of the array if the sum of the denominators is an odd number. Moreover, we demonstrate that the set of fractions with numerator p equal to 2 and denominator q equal to any even number can identify any array with an even sum. Finally, we show that the set of fractions with numerator p equal to 2 and denominator q equal to any odd number cannot determine the sum of the array unless the sum of the denominators is an odd number. In this case, it acts in the same manner as the set of fractions with numerator p equal to any odd number. In the process, we establish a connection between the identifiable sets of fractions and the concept of a specific subset of natural numbers known as'resilient numbers'. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained
considerable popularity in recent years. As MongoDB scales horizontally, it
employs a transactional integrity mechanism to ensure data consistency across
its horizontally scaled architecture. Nonetheless, validating the transactional
integrity of MongoDB within its deployment has not been previously examined in
theoretical or practical terms. In this paper, we present a concise specification
of MongoDB's transactional integrity and a method for validating this property
during execution. Furthermore, we reviewed the source code of MongoDB version
4.2 to align it with the specified property and identified areas where the code
could be improved. As a practical contribution, we developed a tool that can
validate the transactional integrity of MongoDB-4.2 based on its open-source
code, allowing for both dynamic validation during execution and static analysis
using popular tools like SMT solvers or the SPOT model checker. Validation
results indicate that MongoDB-4.2 adheres to the specified property, and our tool
is available for download to enable further investigation of this NoSQL database
integrity.

We've obtained new insights into the solar wind energy flux within the inner region of our solar system.  According to classical theories, the solar wind energy flux should decrease exponentially with distance from the sun due to its dependence on both velocity and temperature components.  However, when we account for the conservation of energy and the solar wind's radial expansion, the predicted decrease should be less pronounced.  Our analysis of data collected during the early stages of the Parker Solar Probe's mission supports the latter prediction, revealing a only gradual reduction in energy flux beneath 0.25 AU.  This finding holds true for both slow and fast solar wind streams.  It also remains consistent when we factor in any possible effects of the solar wind's turbulent temperature fluctuations.  One possible explanation for this observation involves the solar wind's energy distribution patterns near the sun, where we find evidence of a prolonged period of energy conservation throughout the inner heliosphere.  This phenomenon could be linked to the influence of the solar breeze on the solar corona and inner heliosphere.  However, to fully understand this behavior, we require additional insights into the solar wind's energy and conservation dynamics in the inner heliosphere.  Therefore, further analysis of the solar wind's energy and temperature components across a broader range of solar distances is necessary.  This research builds upon the findings reported in Velli et al. (2020), expanding on the results for the energy flux within the inner heliosphere.  It also introduces a new section on the solar wind's temperature components across the inner heliosphere.  Further study on this topic is ongoing as part of the Solar Probe Plus science program. The catalog of the Milky Way bulge's globular clusters remains a subject of debate due to the ambiguity of some clusters whose nature remains uncertain. We have investigated a subset of 19 stars suspected to be part of globular clusters within the bulge using photometric and spectroscopic data. Following the analysis, we found that only four of these stars are likely members of globular clusters - specifically, the omega Centauri type globular cluster $\omega$ Centauri and the globular clusters NGC 64477, NGC 66377, and Ter 4. The remaining clusters are either open clusters, horizontal branch stars, or reddened and polluted asymptotic giant branch stars. This study underscores the difficulty in identifying clusters within the bulge and highlights the necessity for additional data to clarify the nature of these stars. Furthermore, we suggest potential targets for future surveys or observations that could confirm the presence of these four suspected globular clusters. The data utilized in this analysis comprise near-infrared photometry from the VVV survey, combined with spectroscopic data from LAMOST, Gaia, and SDSS. The resulting catalog of the four suspected globular clusters is as follows:

* Name: KSP/N2K/2MASS/J-M/KS
* Values for $\omega$ Centauri: 19.54/8.62/14.49/8.49
* Values for NGC 64477: 17.32/7.44/12.74/7.44
* Values for NGC 66377: 16.87/7.38/12.69/7.38
* Values for Ter 4: 16.51/7.23/11.89/7.23

The likely members of these clusters exhibit horizontal branch loci in color-magnitude diagrams and the LAMOST spectroscopic data reveal them to be low-luminosity horizontal branch stars with metallicity [Fe/H] = -0.76 $\pm$ 0.03. The four clusters have similar spatial distributions within the bulge and the omega Centauri type globular cluster contains the most metal-poor stars among them. The idea that life could be spread across space by panspermia, initially proposed by Hermann Winkler in 1870 and later popularized by Francis Crick in 1981, originates from the observation that life thrives everywhere it is looked for on Earth. To explore the feasibility of discovering microbial life transported through interstellar matter, we examined the characteristics of such life forms and their astronomical signatures. Combining this information with existing and upcoming astronomical detection capabilities, we determined they could identify biosignatures of panspermia in various astrophysical environments by analyzing local star-forming regions, supernovae remnant regions, and globular clusters on the horizon for certain exoplanetary transport methods. In the near future, this may be achievable using current techniques within a decade, depending on the sensitivity of upcoming instruments. In the more distant future, we anticipate the ability to detect viable microorganisms transported through interstellar space across a wide range of environments. The Nernst effect is characterized by an induced thermal voltage in response to a magnetic field application. In ordinary materials, the Nernst effect is counteracted by thermoelectric phenomena, resulting in opposing Peltier and Nernst effects. This phenomenon is known as the Nernst figure of merit, which is less than 1 for all materials. However, researchers have recently found materials where the Nernst figure of merit exceeds 1, indicating unusually large thermal voltage and opposing Peltier effects. These discoveries have been primarily observed in bulk antiferromagnetic materials with complex crystal structures. In this study, the Nernst effect was investigated in thin layers of the antiferromagnetic material Mn$_3$NiN. Unexpected results showed that the Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN is significantly larger than the Peltier effect for the first time observed in an interface. The unique properties of the Mn$_3$NiN interface are attributed to the lack of bulk scattering, accurate measurement of the Peltier coefficient, and unique thermal and magnetic boundary conditions. The results also demonstrate that the Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN is anomalous, as it is normally minimal in thin films due to its similarity to the Seebeck effect. The anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN is primarily caused by the unique geometry of the interface, which generates significant vortex currents and resulting thermal voltage. The results of this study open up the possibility of exploring the Nernst effect in magnetic materials at interfaces and also demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst effect can be utilized in the design of magnetic interface devices. This article presents an innovative approach to solving the Diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ where both $a$ and $b$ are whole numbers. By applying a quadratic transformation, we obtain two distinct equations: $64c^2-1=7d^2$ and $(2c)^2 \pm (2d)b \pm (2c)^2 =7^n$. Leveraging existing results on the first equation, we can establish constraints on the solutions for the second equation, ultimately leading to the conclusion that there are no solutions for $n \le 9$. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for possible solutions of the second equation in terms of $n$, which can be refined to $(n+3)/2$ when $n$ is even. Combining these findings with those from the literature, we are able to state that the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ has no whole number solutions for $n \le 9$ and any solution for $n \ge 10$ must satisfy $n \le (323+14\sqrt7)/2$. Lastly, we provide examples validating this upper bound for $n=11,13,17$ and offer some numerical data on the Pythagorean triples involved. The article also includes an analysis of the related equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ where $a$ and $b$ can take on any integers, uncovering an interesting pattern that may lead to further insights. The innovative transformation used here enables us to explore the structure of the equation's solutions and the article concludes by outlining some open problems arising from this investigation. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when interacting with complex environments. This challenge stems from the difficult trade-off between maintaining stability and achieving high-speed movements, as typically required for forward motion. A key benefit of walking over running or jumping lies in its inherent stability, making it a more practical option for navigating uncertain terrain. This work focuses on the design and development of a biped runner to demonstrate that, with proper design, it's possible to maintain high-speed movements even in the presence of uncertain terrain. By incorporating passive elements into the runner's design, it was possible to leverage the natural stability offered by walking, and the resulting model was validated through physical testing. The proposed design was then used as a basis for a monopod jumper to investigate what benefits passive elements could provide when used in a more compact design. The simulation results revealed that with the appropriate design, it's possible to enhance the height of a single-step jump by as much as fifty percent. Furthermore, the transition from jumping to landing was examined in detail, and the findings showed that passive elements can significantly reduce the height of the center of mass during landing by as much as twenty-five percent, thus providing a level of robustness against uncertain terrain. The proposed design was also compared to other high jump records, including that of a flea, demonstrating that with further optimization, it's possible for the monopod jumper to leap even higher than a flea. The code for the simulator used in this research has been made available online for download. The current record for the highest jump achieved by a monopod jumper stands at fifteen centimeters, and the challenge remains open for others to exceed this record. The research into the mechanics of jumping also provides valuable insights into the difficult problem of interacting with uncertain terrain, offering a promising foundation for further innovation. Knowledge tracing systems based on deep learning have gained significant traction due to their ability to forecast students' knowledge with relative accuracy. As such systems are now being tested in educational settings with real students and significant consequences, it's essential to validate their performance thoroughly. Typically, these systems are evaluated using student data alone. However, this approach overlooks important factors that influence teaching practices and the learning environment, thus complicating the deployment of knowledge tracing technology. To address this challenge, this paper introduces pyKT, a Python-based framework designed to conduct rigorous testing of knowledge tracing systems by integrating mock students with realistic behavior simulated based on existing analytical models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of pyKT by modifying the Knowledge Tracing Graph Convolutional Network model to evaluate its performance when interacting with mock students. As a result, we discovered a previously unreported issue with the KTCG model that manifests as a decline in forecasting accuracy over time as students' engagement patterns become more complex. To rectify this problem, we introduced a temporal attention mechanism that revitalizes the model's performance by enabling it to focus on relevant time periods. As proof of concept, we incorporated the temporal attention mechanism into the KTCG model and tested it on three distinct datasets, thereby validating its practical applications. The code for pyKT, the temporal attention mechanism for KTCG, and associated datasets are available online at https://github.com/kuanghou/pyKT.

This issue can be mitigated by allowing devices to operate independently for extended periods before submitting updates to the server. However, allowing unsupervised gradient updates introduces several challenges, including the potential for gradient discrepancies between the local models and the aggregated global model. This discrepancy can lead to slow convergence rates or even model divergence. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing an unsupervised gradient update method that enables devices to participate in federated learning without restrictions. We also introduce a new algorithm called Buffered Synchronous Aggregation (BSA) to handle large-scale datasets. Our experiments under constrained and unconstrained setups demonstrate that BSA outperforms existing methods significantly. On real-world datasets, BSA reduces the convergence rate gap to a single-round federated block by approximately 30%. On synthetic datasets, BSA achieves a 4 times faster convergence rate than existing methods under unconstrained conditions. Evaluating the variability of accretion in young stellar objects is a critical step in understanding the range of accretion rates within the Sun-Jupiter mass gap. This research examines the accretion of XX Cha using X-shooter and it reveals unusually pronounced fluctuations in accretion. We suggest that XX Cha is distinct from other T Tauri stars that exhibit steady accretion and identify a possible relationship between this variability and the star's slow rotational rate. This finding challenges the prevailing assumption that the range of accretion rates is significantly influenced by rotational energy. Rather, it appears that 20-30% of T Tauri stars display similar internal accretion variability regardless of their rotational rates. This study also examines the potential effects of this variability on the documented range of accretion rates and considers alternative methods of analyzing this data. Ultimately, we conclude that even when taking into account this internal accretion variability, there is still evidence that external factors, such as disk mass and stellar mass, have a limited influence on the range of accretion rates. This result holds weight due to the restricted sample size, and further research is necessary to confirm this finding across a broader population of T Tauri stars. This study adds valuable insights to the study of accretion in young stellar objects and highlights the importance of accounting for the range of internal accretion variability when analyzing this data. This research relies on new and existing data, including previously unpublished X-shooter spectra from 2009 to 2011, and observations from the Extreme Polarizer at the 1.5m telescope in 1995. This study utilizes the PENELLOPE code to analyze these data and examine the range of accretion rates within the Sun-Jupiter mass gap. Offline learning is crucial for developing safe and robust artificial agents by leveraging existing data without requiring extensive online training. Offline learning models often focus on maximizing expected reward while accounting for sparsity and noise in available data. However, existing methods typically assume that reward signals are accurate and abundant, which is not always the case. In many real-world scenarios, especially in collaborative settings, rewards are limited or difficult to obtain, making existing solutions impractical. This paper addresses a key offline learning challenge in multi-agent settings, where only a small number of complete trajectory datasets are available, lacking corresponding reward values. A novel model is proposed that combines reward augmentation using a combination of intrinsic motivation and constrained optimization, enabling effective value function learning even in the absence of explicit reward signals. Experimental results show that the proposed model excels in various offline learning scenarios, including small-data settings with scarce reward information. When two particles are entangled, a measurement affecting one particle necessarily influences the other, regardless of distance. This phenomenon, known as nonlocality or entanglement-based connectivity, has been utilized as a criterion for true nonlocality in multi-particle systems. However, when considering a single particle that has undergone a measurement entanglement with a distant particle, the outcome may become entangled with it, leading to a new interpretation of this situation. If this particle has then been used as a means to guide another particle to the other end, we could then say that the initial particle's measurement has an nonlocal effect on the distant particle. In this study, we outline a specific scenario in which measuring a particular property of this particle will necessarily affect the behavior of a second particle at the other end, even when the two particles are located far apart. The nonlocal impact of this measurement on the second particle can be seen in the way it reduces the probability of the particle behaving in a particular manner. Consequently, even when just one particle has been measured to become entangled with the distant particle, this can result in a nonlocal effect on the behavior of the other particle. As a result, even in a system made up of just two particles, we now have the possibility of true nonlocality existing within just one particle. We have also discovered a method to quantify this nonlocality, describing it in terms of the probability of the particle behaving in a particular manner. The reduction of this probability is directly related to the degree of nonlocality existing within the particle. The phenomenon of single-particle nonlocality can be achieved through the use of a specific entangled state, and it remains stable even when the particle has interacted with its surroundings. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that even in a system with three particles, single-particle nonlocality can result from the entanglement between just two particles, indicating that it is possible for just one particle to exhibit nonlocal behavior even in a system made up of many particles. The possibility of just one particle behaving in this manner following a measurement entanglement with the other particles also raises the possibility of using this phenomenon for the purpose of guiding a particle to the other end of a system, providing it with a specific property, and it does so with a degree of precision that is directly related to the degree of nonlocality existing within the particle. V392 Persei, observed in 2018, is considered one of the most radiant novae in nearly four decades, with nova radiation extending to gamma-rays. This outbreak from a small nova that had previously exploded in 1966 suggests a remarkably long period of activity for a nova of this type. To understand this phenomenon, we examined the spectral characteristics of its ejected particles and found that the nova particles emitted high-energy electrons and heavy ions at exceptional levels. These findings indicate that the gamma-rays originated from the interaction of these particles with the surrounding interstellar gas, specifically in the constellation of Perseus. Furthermore, we discovered that the nova particles emitted significant amounts of protons, making this the first observed case of a small nova producing abundant cosmic rays. Lastly, we observed the ongoing radiation from the nova site over time, revealing that the outbreak had a more prolonged period of activity than typically seen in novae. We considered nuclear star clusters at the centers of early-type galaxies and analyzed their possible formation scenarios through gravitational wave events. For the most likely scenario - formed like globular clusters with rapid star formation in the early universe - we found that even a single nuclear star cluster in a massive galaxy could generate a gravitational wave signal below the LISA detection limit. However, formed like globular clusters with slow star formation in the early universe, such clusters would produce a strong signal only if they contain a retained black hole of at least 40 solar masses. This could result in hundreds of detectable signals in the LISA era. For a typical Milky Way nuclear star cluster, we calculate its total signal amplitude as less than $3.7\times 10^{-14}$ ergs of energy in the LISA band, indicating that only a small fraction of detected sources will be identified as nuclear star clusters. Yet, this prediction suggests that a significant portion of LISA's detected sources may be associated with the early universe. Additionally, we anticipate findings for a few clusters that hosted three to five binary mergers, which would allow for sub-clusters mass estimation and influence on globular cluster formation during the early universe. Lastly, in these dense environments, binary mergers may occur through dynamical interactions instead of binary evolution, which could result in mergers involving black holes of at least 5 solar masses and neutron stars of at least 1.5 solar masses. This could divide the LISA signal from nuclear star clusters from that from binary evolution sources. If possible, distinguishing between these two groups could significantly enhance the understanding of the early universe.

Text-based games provide a rigorous testing ground for natural language interactions, requiring players to navigate a world via commands and receive descriptive responses.
However, executing these interactions is notoriously slow due to the manual process of inputting commands and updating the world, making it impractical for high-speed evaluation.
To address this limitation, we present TextWorldExpress, a unified framework for TextWorld tasks that enables us to accelerate interactions by emulating the effects of commands on the world.
Our simulator leverages cutting-edge techniques from reinforcement learning, real-world games, and physics-based simulation to generate responsive environments for text-based games.
We demonstrate the speed and effectiveness of our TextWorldExpress platform across multiple benchmarks, including the Hidden Room, TextAdventure, and Visions of the Deep challenges.
In particular, we show that it is possible to evaluate agents on commonly used text-based game benchmarks at speeds of up to one million interactions per second.
To facilitate further advancement in natural language processing interactions, we open-source the TextWorldExpress simulator alongside a comprehensive methodology for creating compatible Hidden Room levels.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can display
nonlinear phenomena in quantum mechanics. We introduce a new idea where a linear
operator is elevated to a higher order to create a nontrivial effect in a quantum
system. In this study, we develop a linear operator with an elevated order that is
analogue to Weyl semimetals and investigate its implications in both infinite and
finite systems. We demonstrate that certain "Fermi arcs" reappear, and our results
also indicate that the nontrivial effect caused by the elevated order vanishes at
the points of mass generation. In addition, we examine the effect of an external
magnetic field and discover that it transforms the elevated order from a "soccer
ball" shape into a "rugby ball" shape. Our findings suggest that overloading the
elevated order could generate a topological phase in both infinite and finite systems. 
Our research indicates that it is feasible to experimentally realize this novel
elevated-order quantum state in moiré materials formed by stacking graphene layers. 
Our calculations also demonstrate that an external electric field can be used to 
tune the elevated order in these moiré materials. In conclusion, this study provides
a theoretical framework for understanding both general and specific elevated-order 
quantum systems. We anticipate that our research will open up theoretical avenues 
for investigating other nonlinear operator analogues of exotic quantum phenomena. 
Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenghuiLeng/SRW.

This paper focuses on the long-term development of Venus's atmosphere, examining how chemical compounds in the atmosphere influence atmospheric processes and contribute to climate evolution through interactions with biological and geological systems. To explore this, we divided the atmosphere's chemical compartment into five categories: gases, aerosols, clouds, fog, and soil-residual compounds. Each category has its own processes and feedback loops that shape the atmosphere and influence atmospheric processes and Earth system evolution. We found that the atmosphere's processes and feedback loops are prolonged over time with various compounds persisting for tens of thousands to millions of years. This longevity supports the idea that extreme conditions aren't sufficient to prevent chemical compounds from evolving over time and interacting with life and geology. As a result, the atmosphere's processes and feedback loops retain their complex, systemically integrated characteristics, with compounds in the atmosphere continuing to influence geological and biological systems at depth. This suggests that any theory seeking to explain the atmosphere's development and Earth system evolution must consider the interactions between chemical compounds, life, and geology over extended time periods. This work was conducted as part of the Biomineralization and Planetary Evolution Project. The project is focused on studying interactions between chemical compounds, life, and geology, with particular interest in the Earth system's biomineralization component, and how it shapes the atmosphere, influences climate evolution, and contributes to Earth system evolution over extended time periods. The project's findings have implications for understanding the interactions that formed the Earth's crust, atmospheric processes, and life, as well as similar interactions on Mars and other planets. The project also offers methods for studying interactions between life, geology, and atmospheric processes on other planets based on chemical compound analysis in the atmosphere, with potential applications in astrobiology. The project's researchers are composed of biologists, geologists, atmospheric scientists, planetary scientists, and astrobiologists working together to study interactions between life, geology, and atmospheric processes, with the aim of contributing to ongoing efforts in astrobiology, planetary science, and the search for life on Mars and other planets. The first metric related to the predictive power of the model, and the second metric related to the diversity of the clusters. We have conducted simulated experiments to evaluate our method and compared it to the alternative method of using variational Bayesian approximation. Furthermore, we have applied our method to a real-world dataset of Twitter posts. We have also discussed some of the method's limitations and possible solutions. A proposed approach involves the use of magnetized plasmas that could modify a laser pulse's polarization to align with its direction of propagation, potentially allowing for more intense focus without material destruction. However, the predicted effects are very small, around 10^-3, which is not sufficient for achieving the necessary intensity in laboratory settings. A proposed model modifies the magnetized plasma model by incorporating free electrons' influence on the polarization change, leading to a predicted increase in the effect size by a factor of 10^5. This results in a modifiable degree of polarization that can reach 1 as the laser intensity approaches 10^24 W/cm^2, which is capable of focusing the full energy of a 100 J, 100 femtosecond laser without material damage. Verifying news accuracy has become increasingly difficult in the digital age due to the overwhelming amount of information posted online. False news spreads quickly, causing harm to individuals, societies, and even leading to physical consequences. To combat this issue, effective methods are necessary to identify and counter false news. One key challenge in this endeavor is the vast quantity of online articles, making it impractical to thoroughly investigate each one. As such, we are looking for ways to efficiently determine which articles are worth further investigation. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that leverages text condensation to create a compact version of articles, which can be analyzed using machine learning techniques to develop a false news detection model. We further explore the integration of multiple models, combining their individual predictions to enhance the overall performance. Experimental results reveal that our proposed method outperforms the baseline in three distinct datasets. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal text condensation method and explore the influence of hyperparameters on the dataset used. As such, this proposed framework is suitable for false news detection across various domains. The code for this study is available open-source on GitHub at https://github.com/TextCondensation/FCN-TC. Moreover, a web application has been developed in conjunction with this research, allowing users to upload articles for false news detection. Details regarding this application, known as FalseNewsDetector, can be found at https://false-news-detector.herokuapp.com/. This proposed method has several implications for the prevention of false news, including educational programs that teach users about the effectiveness of machine learning-based article compression, as well as strategic placement of paid advertisements to increase the efficacy of the web application. Lastly, we discuss potential avenues for further research, including the integration of user feedback into the model, as well as the development of a dataset specifically tailored to false news detection. Unlike the traditional approach using eigenvalues and eigenvectors from the data covariance matrix, which is susceptible to failure or significant computational costs when the number of vectors exceeds the dimensionality, we propose alternative methods. These proposals involve minimizing the sum of the $\ell_1$-norm distances from each vector to a linear transformation of the principal component, subject to constraints on the rotation group. Additionally, we show the linear convergence of our proposed optimization algorithms and provide a theoretical framework for their analysis. This analysis highlights the optimal parameters required to ensure the algorithm maintains its linear convergence properties as it solves more complex problems. This research also contributes a novel understanding of the $\ell_1$-norm geodesic distance on the rotation group, which has implications for the optimization algorithms used. In recent years, AI models have significantly improved at asking follow-up questions, a crucial aspect of conversational dialogue. To evaluate these models, researchers created the Follow-up Question Generation dataset, which contains pairs of initial and follow-up questions. However, simply generating any suitable follow-up isn't sufficient; the challenge lies in creating precise next questions that address a particular issue, such as identifying a character's emotion in a story. To tackle this problem, a dataset is proposed that includes both narrative texts and initial questions with designated answer tags, making it possible to assess generated follow-up questions against these standards. Specifically for the emotion-related questions, they focus on questions that ask about a character's emotional state. To evaluate the generated follow-up questions, semantic tagging adjustment is proposed, effectively rewriting the initial question's tags to match the generated follow-up. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, it was applied to already existing datasets, resulting in higher scores when evaluating generated follow-up questions against human-created pairs. Furthermore, an analysis is presented highlighting the challenges of conditionally generating question tags. For robots to effectively navigate complex environments on their own, having a solid grasp of the surroundings topology is crucial. In this paper, a new method for representing environments using HiTMaps is proposed. This hierarchical approach organizes spatial data into multiple layers, each dealing with a distinct aspect of the environment's topology. By gradually building up from basic mapping components, a hierarchical framework is created that facilitates efficient navigation by leveraging insights from both global and local mapping features. In contrast to conventional mapping approaches, HiTMaps disregard the precise coordinates of landmarks, instead focusing on their relative positions, which simplifies the representation without sacrificing navigational accuracy. Moreover, a motion prediction module is introduced to anticipate future robot movements based on the mapped representation, ensuring the representation remains accurate and up-to-date. The proposed method is put to the test in simulation scenarios and real-world deployments, outperforming non-hierarchical topological navigation methods in terms of computation time and motion prediction accuracy. HiTMaps have the potential to be integrated into a variety of mapping approaches and offer a flexible framework for representing and navigating dynamic and unfamiliar environments. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring minute variations in local magnetic fields. Metrological techniques such as atomic interferometry offer high sensitivity to this task, however, they are typically limited to detecting changes in electric potential rather than magnetic fields. That said, there is an interesting twist - the precise control over electromagnetic properties in superconducting materials through interference patterns generated by atomic beams can actually allow for the measurement of magnetic fields. Here, we explore this concept further and outline a specific approach using nickel-coated nitrogen vapors in an atomic interferometer setup. This setup would leverage the unique property of superconductors to repel magnetic fields (the Meissner effect) so that when a superconducting nickel coil is brought close to the nitrogens, even the tiniest changes in the magnetic field between the nitrogens and the nickel coil during and after it becomes superconducting could be accurately measured. Our calculations indicate this method could achieve an impressive level of field detection with values as low as $10^{-12}$ Tesla. Moreover, this approach would also enable the study of superconducting materials' property known as the lower critical field, which has significant implications for both condensed matter and quantum physics. Not to mention, this method could be scaled up to detect magnetic fields in larger objects, including living organisms. The required technology is currently available and only needs minor adjustments, therefore it's feasible to execute this approach in the near future. In essence, this approach offers a groundbreaking way to measure local magnetic fields with atomic interferometry, and as such, it has the potential to revolutionize not just metrology but also a wide range of scientific disciplines including biology, chemistry, and physics. The potential applications of this technique are vast and we outline some of the key ones in this paper, however, it's worth noting that the scope of these applications is limitless as this technique can detect any alteration in the magnetic field around any object. The approach we outline in this paper could also serve as the foundation for measuring changes in electric potential, as well as detecting changes in spatial location, simply by moving the nitrogens further away from the nickel coil. The level of detection this approach offers is so precise that it can even facilitate the identification of specific subatomic particles that have unique magnetic properties, as well as the detection of subtle movements in space, as long as they occur in close proximity to the nitrogens. Mixtures of distributions constitute a versatile tool that can be used to model data consisting of multiple components by employing a parametric probability distribution as the mixture model. We demonstrate that any finite mixture model is equivalent to a mixture process of geometric probability measures defined over a polytope, which can be viewed as a variation of the classical mixture model idea. We establish this connection using a representation of mixtures based on the principles of stochastic geometry and Choquet theory. This geometric framework provides an alternative interpretation of parametric mixture models and offers potential advantages in terms of model development and inference. Specifically, we show that mixtures models can be treated as mixture processes of geometric probability measures, which enables the use of closure and convex combination operations to extend the models to infinite mixtures, and provides an alternative to inference methods based on optimization techniques. Moreover, this geometric perspective can be applied to model development through the use of support vector machines, and facilitates the computation of mixture model quantities through numerical integration. We also include a specific application to the classification problem, along with a discussion of the model's performance in comparison to non-geometric alternatives. In this context, we introduce a new measure of model performance based on the Lovasz theta function, which can be computed efficiently. In addition, we provide a concise overview, accessible to a broader audience, of the key elements of stochastic geometry and Choquet theory in the appendix. In the appendix, we also examine the relationship between mixtures models and geometric probability measures in the special case of bivariate data. In this case, we graphically visualize the mixtures models as non-crossing partitions of the unit square, which provides a simple and intuitive visualization of the model components. We also discuss the connection between mixtures models and non-crossing partitions of general polytopes in the appendix. In the appendix, we further examine the relationship between mixtures models and geometric probability measures using the sandpile model, which enables the computation of the measure of small cells. We demonstrate that mixtures models can be treated as mixture processes of geometric probability measures defined over a graph, which enables the use of numerical methods based on the Laplacian of the adjacency matrix of the graph to extend the models to infinite mixtures. In this context, we introduce a new measure of the complexity of graphs, which provides an alternative to the Colin de Verdiere number. In the appendix, we also examine the relationship between mixtures models and geometric probability measures defined over a tree, which enables the computation of the measure of the branches of the tree.

High-performance computing on GPUs is increasingly effective but has a significant obstacle to overcome - limited memory availability. In OpenACC, memory is allocated before computations take place, but there's a lack of tools that efficiently manage memory on a large scale during parallel object-based programming. In response to this challenge, we present DynaSOAr, a state-of-the-art, thread-safe memory allocator for OpenACC on GPUs with enhanced memory management capabilities. Unlike existing methods, DynaSOAr can dynamically allocate memory on a large scale during computations and on a per-thread basis to prevent interference between threads. Furthermore, DynaSOAr features over 2 times performance improvement and memory savings of up to 1.9GB when running real-world applications. We also introduce a new approach, called sparse object arrays, that allows for efficient memory allocation and provide extensive usage examples in our supplementary materials. DynaSOAr is an advanced memory allocator that outperforms existing methods and our code is publicly available.

A theoretical framework for the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states that forms between a quasiparticle and a localized magnetic impurity on a superconducting surface has been developed. This model, supported by an initial principles method, accurately describes local magnetic moments's influence on the YSR states. It was found that the YSR states's behavior in a chain of dimers is governed by both the inter- and the intra-dimer interactions. This theoretical analysis was applied to both an Mn adatom and Mn dimers on a Nb(110) surface, and it was discovered that YSR states's binding energies in a chain of dimers exhibit both inter- and intra-dimer interactions, which could be either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic. This theory was compared to experimental data obtained using a low-temperature scanning tunneling microscope, and it was found that it accurately describes the behavior of YSR states in both cases. This theoretical analysis also highlights the importance of considering both the inter- and the intra-dimer interactions in a chain of YSR states's binding energies in order to accurately describe their behavior in both cases. This finding provides further evidence for the magnetic dipole-dipole interaction's role in determining the YSR states's behavior in a chain of dimers.
