The NASA's TESS mission has allowed for a more complete picture of exoplanetary systems similar to our own solar system.  While most known exoplanetary systems contain large gas giants on one side and small terrestrial planets on the other, there is still a gap in data regarding systems containing at least two mini-Neptunes within the habitable zones of their stars.  We report the discovery of three mini-Neptunes orbiting TOI-712, a 10.5 Gyr star that is part of an astrometric cluster with the same proper motion as the Alpha Centauri system and is likely very similar in metallicity.  With masses between 20 and 40 times that of Earth, the two outer planets in the system show nearly circular orbits while the third planet's orbit is more elliptical.  This system offers valuable insights into the formation of mini-Neptunes and highlights the diversity of exoplanetary systems similar to our own.  With a stellar spin rate that is lower than expected, TOI-712 may also provide insight into the relationships between stellar spin, planetary systems and the chemical composition of stars.  With a juvinile rotation rate, this star may have 1.5 Gyr left before it becomes a subgiant.  As such, this system offers a compelling argument for continued study with instruments such as the ESPA spectrograph and future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope. By leveraging vector boson production in the forward direction, the proposed method aims to identify an anomalous increase in the number of elastic events with large rapidity separations, a characteristic signature of this process. This strategy, which utilizes data collected by the CMS experiment, specifically utilises proton-proton collision data at an energy of 13.6 TeV and incorporates advanced techniques to effectively search for the phenomenon across a broad range of elastic scattering processes. The resulting elastic cross-section for top quark pairs can be determined with some uncertainty, and this approach has the potential to provide the first direct measurement of this quantity with a precision of around 30%. Furthermore, as the phenomenon under investigation shares many similarities with that of Higgs production via vector boson fusion, this research may also contribute to better understanding this related process, often considered a crucial background in searches for new physics but with a rather narrowly defined signature. The proposed analysis strategy has been implemented and tested using simulated data, and the resulting methodology has been validated against existing research on the subject. The resulting experimental limits on the elastic top quark scattering cross-section are found to be quite precise, with a precision of around 30%. A significant aspect they identified involves characterizing infinite graphs whose subgraphs conform to a specified pattern hold within every two-coloring of the countably infinite grid. These graphs are referred to as being deeply Ramsey. A key question posed by them seeks the Ramsey properties of the infinite binary tree structure. Recently, a class of non-abelian gauge theories known as scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in (1+1) dimensions have been successfully simulated using qudits with various trimerizations. These simulations can either use closed systems to produce periodic signals or closed systems to generate signal fragments. Due to the complexity of the spectrum in closed systems, some "hidden" resonances with large signal amplitudes can go undetected unless specific careful searches are conducted. This study examined the simulation of sQED using qudits in closed systems with trimerizations other than the standard trichromatism. A general method for simulating this model was developed, and it was discovered that trichromatism can significantly influence the amplitude of certain resonances, making some qudits much more effective at simulating sQED. In fact, one qudit, the tritetrachromatism, was found to possess a resonance with an exceptionally large amplitude, surpassing the amplitude of the corresponding resonance in the standard trichromatism qudit by an incredible 250 times after adjusting for detuning. In addition, it was discovered that trichromatism can also influence the system's dynamics by displacing the resonances' frequency and altering their widths. As a result, there are many untapped possibilities for improving qudit simulations simply by switching to a different trichromatism, and researchers are now advised to provide detailed information about their trichromatism when sharing simulation data. Moreover, qudits with dynamic trichromatism, which can change over time, have been discovered and proven to be a valuable tool for simultaneously avoiding resonances while increasing the signal amplitude. In conclusion, this study has unlocked several valuable insights that are relevant to a broad range of simulations, including but not limited to sQED. A trichromatism- amplitude dictionary has been created and is available for download. A trichromatism controller has been developed for dynamic trichromatism simulations. Both of these tools are highly customizable and can be used in a wide range of simulations. In the context of ultra-relativistic, intense laser-electron colliders, we are investigating the effects of intense light on high-energy positrons that are produced through the interaction of a positron and an intense laser shining on a thin target. We find that the polarization of these positrons can exceed 10% due to their strong acceleration during the interaction process. Moreover, by increasing the thickness of the target, we discover that the produced positron bunches become remarkably long, extending up to several centimeters, and exhibit remarkable characteristics such as wide distribution of polarization, both longitudinal and angular. We also discuss the implications of using a thick target and identify areas such as particle beam recycling and retroreflectors that could be beneficial in this setup. Additionally, we investigate the underlying structural characteristics of these computationally effective majority-of-gates functions and demonstrate that they comprise a distinct and distinctively complex class of functions that cannot be categorized within the broader category of regular functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the presence of function circuits with a limited basis at a particular, albeit minimal, depth level is both necessary and sufficient for defining these complex majority-of-gates functions. A corresponding time complexity result is also derived. A crucial aspect of our current research is the discovery of a specific, well-defined parameter that can be used to characterize the underlying structure of these computationally effective majority-of-gates functions, and this parameter is found to be provably 'frugal' in its nature. This research develops a miniature temperature detector using a fully differential architecture, enabling precise thermal measurements while minimizing voltage supply requirements. The temperature sensor employs a single PMOS transistor characterizing temperature changes in its threshold voltage, body effect, and sub-threshold current. By analyzing these factors, a single, linear temperature coefficient is calculated and used to create a temperature estimation algorithm. The proposed design was implemented in a 65nm CMOS process, with a 0.24°C precision achieved over the 0°C to 85°C operating range and only ±1.4°C error occurring outside this range. The temperature detector's operational voltage range spans from 0.6V to 1.8V, with a sub-milliwatt average power consumption during temperature measurements. The miniaturized design occupies a minimal area of 0.024mm². The proposed temperature detector was tested on a flexible circuit board using varying supply voltages, with results verified through both simulation and hardware experimentation. A corresponding SPICE model is provided for research reproduction purposes. A custom-built prototype demonstrated the miniaturized temperature detector's effectiveness in various applications. A discussion on the design's limitations and potential solutions is also presented. A differential inductive sensing temperature detector alternative is introduced, with the same research team, for comparison purposes. The proposed design's precision, accuracy, and power consumption make it suitable for low-power wireless sensor networks, with the code available on GitHub. This research paper explores two main concepts: geometric configurations on Lie groupoids and geometric configurations on stacks. It begins by introducing precise definitions for these configurations and identifying their key properties. Next, it classifies configuration properties into two categories: intrinsic properties, which remain consistent under morphisms from a stack to the space of configurations, and extrinsic properties, which do not share this stability trait. The paper then delves into the examination of intrinsic properties among geometric configurations on Lie groupoids and stacks through isomorphism invariants. This involves examining whether these properties can be determined by presheaves that recognize stack properties. Alongside this analysis, the paper also investigates specific intrinsic configuration properties, including integrability, submersiveness, and transitivity. Furthermore, it provides concrete examples to demonstrate how these properties behave under different groupoid representations. The paper's final section connects these concepts to the realm of germs of distributions and symplectic groupoids. The development of configuration spaces is also influenced by stack invariants, and the paper demonstrates this through the examination of a specific example involving the symplectic groupoid associated with a Neumann extension. This example showcases how the behavior of configuration spaces changes when the underlying space changes from compact to non-compact. The paper's findings also highlight the importance of distinguishing between compact and non-compact settings when studying distributional properties. The term "distributional properties" is used here to describe intrinsic configuration properties that can be determined by presheaves that recognize stack properties along distributions. A statistical study of 106 far-infrared dark nebulae, incorporating data from IRAS, Planck, and Herschel, is presented.  The research focuses on the core properties of these nebulae, utilizing submillimeter continuum data from the Submillimeter Array and 16 GHz methanol masers as a star formation indicator.  A comparison with the Planck thermal dust emission allows for the derivation of core masses and radii for the dark cores.  The analysis reveals a correlation between the expansion velocity of dark cores and their mass, with values ranging from 0.2 to 3.5 km/s.  The study further examines the physical properties of dark cores, revealing a transition mass of $ \sim 30$ M$_{\sun}$\ below which the cores exhibit supersonic motion, while more massive cores show sonic motion.  The research also explores the relationship between dark cores and the surrounding environment, using the Planck column density map to analyze the properties of dark cores in different molecular complexes.  The study identifies the Dragon complex as a particular example, characterized by a range of core masses and densities, with some cores displaying sonic motion and others with supersonic motion.  The analysis of the Dragon complex further resolves its core mass function into two separate distributions, with different mass thresholds for the two components.  The research explains the absence of high-mass star formation in the Dragon complex by referencing the high core mass dispersion and lack of dense cores with masses above 30 M$_{\sun}$.  The study also examines the spatial distribution of the complex's core masses and densities, with a peak found at a cloud core mass of $ \sim 10^{3}$ M$_{\sun}$.  The analysis divides the complex into four separate components, with different mass and density properties, including a dense infrared bright core surrounded by less dense material.  The research further examines the velocity dispersions of the Dragon complex's cores, with values ranging from 0.5 to 3.5 km/s, and a peak found at a cloud core velocity dispersion of $ \sim 2$ km/s.  The analysis of the velocity dispersions reveals a relationship with the core's surrounding environment, with the velocity dispersions influenced by the surrounding magnetic field and gravitational forces.  The study discusses the importance of magnetic fields and gravity in regulating the velocity dispersions, with self-gravity playing a more significant role in determining the core's velocity dispersion. The flow of liquids through narrow channels is inherently difficult due to friction, and this challenge is compounded in porous media like soap froths. To better understand the obstacles foam molecules encounter during flow, our experiments using a controlled channeling system revealed the importance of surface roughness in the froth's tubes of flow. We found that even a small degree of surface roughness can cause deflection and sticking of foam molecules, significantly hindering their movement. As a result, the required pressure to drive the flow increases exponentially with the roughness of the tubes. To further explore this phenomenon, we incorporated surface roughness into the lubrication model, obtaining insights that align with our experimental findings. In the process, we also identified a critical dimensionless ratio that determines the transition from stick-slip behavior to smooth tube flow. To extend our discoveries to natural porous media like sand, we proposed a roughness-induced resistance model and successfully applied it to the tubes of a sand foam system. In doing so, we demonstrated the potential for surface roughness to influence flow through natural media, with implications for various geological and biological processes. With this research, we have taken an initial step towards integrating the effects of surface roughness and geometry in the tubes of flow, with the goal of further refining the model to include variations in tube diameter and the presence of surface chemical interactions. In its present form, however, our model remains a valuable tool for analyzing the resistance driven by surface roughness in the tubes of flow. To facilitate replication and exploration of this research, we have incorporated the parameters and dimensions of our experiments into an appendix. With its focus on the intricate relationships between surface roughness, tube diameter, and flow resistance, this study offers contributions to the fields of geomechanics, hydrology, and biology, with potential applications to various natural and biological processes. In neural machine translation, a common method to generate high-quality outputs is the look-ahead focus approach, which involves creating a separate decoder to predict desired output characteristics, then using those characteristics to guide the primary decoder. To address this challenge, researchers propose a novel method called the look-ahead focus for creation framework, which allows users to specify the number of desired output components and their corresponding structures. A key feature of this framework is the ability to condition the primary decoder on multiple focal decoders, each responsible for generating a different output component. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the researchers focused on neural machine translation with nested structure outputs and achieved state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, the proposed framework is versatile and can be applied to various creation tasks in the machine translation domain. Moreover, the proposed framework has been tested on NMTCG datasets, namely the BDT dataset and the NMTCG-NYTimes dataset, with promising results. The computational requirements for complex biological simulations exceeded the capabilities of a single desktop computer, leading researchers to explore distributed processing techniques. Based on a grid computing approach, the BioSim grid was designed to manage and optimize high-throughput biological data analysis. A translational method was employed to adapt grid computing to this application, involving the direct implementation of bioinformatics algorithms within the framework. This paper discusses the development of the BioSim grid, focusing on the design of its core components and the integration of a workflow engine to streamline data analysis. The resulting system outperformed a standalone desktop execution of the same simulation by nearly 12 times. Although the BioSim grid was initially intended for a specific purpose, its design is versatile and may be suitable for other similar grid projects. The source code for the BioSim grid is available under the Apache Open Source License. The BioSim grid has the potential to handle more demanding simulations by integrating multiple grid environments, and the development of a frontend tool would further enhance user experience. The research underlying this paper has been published in the Journal of Computational Biology, while the development and implementation of the BioSim grid are detailed in the Journal of Grid Computing. The BioSim grid has been successfully put into production, managing up to 500 active user accounts and securely integrating with various identity management systems via Shibboleth. The BioSim grid has the potential to serve as a prototype for other grid applications developed using a similar translational method. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light neutrinos and dark energy. We update the cross-section and form factors of the J/ψ particle decay into two photons and one neutrino based on the Chern-Simons gauge theory, and determine the neutrino's electric and magnetic moments. We also explore the impact on the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, modifying the J/ψ particle's form factors and providing constraints on the coefficients of neutrino and dark energy effective operators. Specifically, we derive the relationship between the neutrino's magnetic moment and the coefficient of the neutrino dipole moment operator, and identify the neutrino dipole moment operator as a subset of the photon neutrino effective operator with a specific helicity configuration. Consequently, the J/ψ particle's decay into invisible matter allows for more precise measurements of the neutrino's electric and magnetic moments, with improvements of three to four orders of magnitude. Furthermore, this decay also provides constraints on the dark energy scalar's coupling to the photon and fermions with additional helicity constraints, with limits on the coefficients of neutrino and dark energy effective operators at or below the level of 10^-5. Finally, we highlight the importance of incorporating the J/ψ particle's decay into invisible matter into the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, with implications for experiments at proton-proton colliders. With the expected luminosity for upcoming experiments, we anticipate achieving sensitivity to coefficients as low as 10^-5, with potential for further improvements as the number of collected events increases. Consequently, we recommend incorporating the J/ψ particle's decay into invisible matter into effective field theories to ensure accurate interpretations of future data. With the J/ψ particle at the center, we discuss three interpretations of its decay into invisible matter: light efficient neutrino, dark efficient neutrino, and light dark energy. Consequently, we prioritize light efficient neutrino in our analyses, with results applicable to the other two interpretations. This research investigates the long-term behavior of a stochastic process where the time it takes to reach a certain level from a randomly generated initial starting point is considered. Unlike typical models where the focus is on how long it takes to reach a level from a fixed initial point, this model examines the distribution of time it takes to reach the level from a wide range of possible initial points. The complexity of the model leads to us examining its expectations under different mixing conditions of the random initial starting point. Two distinct models are studied: a simple random walk on a finite graph and a fractional Brownian motion with varying levels of self-similarity. The analysis of the models leads to various convergence properties and the existence of a stationary distribution that can be characterized through its moments. The study also compares the models through the moment properties and finds that there are differences in the types of moments that converge and their rates of convergence. However, the transparent functioning of these networks has not been as readily uncovered as their classification performance. Current GCNN implementations rely on extensive empirical testing to pinpoint optimal parameters, which hinders understanding of the networks' fundamental workings. This paper introduces an analytical approach to delving into the inner mechanics of GCNNs by drawing a formal equivalence between their convolution operations and a specific linear filtering process. This equivalence enables precise control over the networks' behavior through carefully designed experiments. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the basic GCNN consists of a linear filtering step followed by a ReLU activation function, which essentially acts as a thresholding operator that determines which data features are incorporated into the networks. Furthermore, this analysis reveals the crucial impact of connected graph matrices on local data features and provides insights into how connectedness affects the networks' ability to generalize. Moreover, this study proposes a new GCNN architecture, termed Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Neural Network, which incorporates both spatial and temporal information into the networks. This architecture outperforms existing GCNN baselines in tasks such as node classification in dynamic social media platforms. We then examine the world defined by this system for its inherent consistency, discovering that it isn't fundamentally consistent. In response, we modify the system to make its world more consistent, albeit at the cost of making truth a relative concept. Ultimately, we show that even with this adjustment, the system cannot be considered fundamentally reliable in defining what is true. This finding leads us to contemplate the implications for the practice of logic-based world-building. Lastly, we conclude by examining the system's connection to a specific problem known as the "Godel world problem." This paper investigates surface stability in fractional-order dynamical systems. It first explains that a specific type of surface, known as an invariant surface or a first integral, can reduce the complexity of a given dynamical system from one fractional dimension to another fraction that is lower than the original. However, for systems with specific fractional dimensions, such as those of order one point five, even when they are hyperbolic, researchers have found that there are no invariant surfaces. The interstellar medium between stars is viewed as a complex, dynamic system influenced by local and global factors. While interstellar scintillation helps reveal the properties of pulsars and the surrounding medium, its study is hindered by requiring simultaneous data from multiple radio telescopes. This paper analyzes long-term data from single-dish observations with the Arecibo telescope, focusing on the scintillation properties of the pulsar B1133+16. By modeling the subpulse patterns and analyzing the wide-band scintillation properties, we identified several components of the interstellar medium along the line of sight to the pulsar. Specifically, we found large-scale scintillation properties to be similar to those of nearby pulsars with similar frequencies, while the properties of the small-scale scintillation components vary significantly. Furthermore, we discovered a component with a large dispersion measure compared to its scintillation bandwidth, which we interpret as a propagating interstellar scintillation pattern from a nearby pulsar wind nebula. This nebula's proximity is inferred to be less than 30 parsecs, which we consider plausible given the observed properties and assumptions about the nebula's structure. This study highlights the value of long-term single-dish observations in investigating the interstellar medium, which can reveal the properties of the medium along a line of sight with high spatial resolution. We also propose a method for recovering interstellar scintillation patterns from single-dish data based on the properties of pulsar emission and the distribution of the interstellar medium. This approach is applicable to data from single-dish telescopes and can be combined with global interferometric data to recover high-resolution maps of the interstellar medium along a line of sight. This technique is particularly useful for recovering the properties of the interstellar medium in crowded regions near the Galactic plane. We anticipate that this method will be highly effective for future large-scale single-dish pulsar monitoring projects, which will greatly increase the number of available data sets. This study is also relevant to the Pulsar Monitoring System currently under development, which will enable real-time analysis of global interferometric data and recover interstellar scintillation patterns from single-dish data based on the properties of pulsar emission and the distribution of the interstellar medium. This approach is anticipated to significantly enhance the accuracy of various pulsar monitoring analyses, which can be applied to a wide range of scientific studies, from astrophysical to biomedical. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with pitch-sensitive dilated convolution layers that incorporate a non-linear combination of multiple convolution filters with different dilation factors, allowing the model to adapt to varying signal periods automatically. Furthermore, a modified version of the WN loss function is introduced to prevent overfitting in the training process. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate its superiority over WN in terms of frequency generalization capability and quality of generated signals in non-overlapping areas. Recent advancements in large-scale graph data processing have led to a growing interest in graph neural networks, which have been successfully applied in various tasks including node classification, link prediction, and molecular design. However, existing GNN models have been trained primarily on large data sets with simple labelings. In contrast, many real-world problems involve complex and uncertain data, necessitating the development of robust methods to handle open-set and meta-learning scenarios. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel GNN architecture, named Lorentzian GNN (LGNN), that builds on the principles of Lorentzian geometry to provide a robust framework for learning on uncertain and dynamic graphs. By leveraging LGNN, we are able to reformulate key GNN operations using the Lorentzian metric, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a range of tasks including open-reconnaissance, in both transductive and semi-supervised settings. Furthermore, LGNN is able to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in both synthetic and real-world experiments. Moreover, we show that LGNN is able to learn from meta-tasks by introducing a dynamic Lorentzian metric, and provide a theoretical analysis of its convergence properties. Lastly, we provide LGNN as a scalable open-source framework for large-scale learning on uncertain graphs. Code is available at: https://github.com/salestock/LGNN.
